Mr. Chairman, at this stage I want to add a few words to some of the suggestions made by hon. members of this group during the course of this economic debate. I appreciate that a great deal of ground has already been covered by a good many hon. members, but I want to try to deal with some points which, in my belief, are of importance to our country and which have not yet had the attention from the government which they should have had.
It is of course true that economic conditions in Canada have improved this year, and the Minister of Finance derived a great deal of satisfaction out of that. It would be rather mean to begrudge him the little bit of consolation he could get out of a rather difficult situation and difficult task, but the fact is that the year 1962 represents the upswing of the economic cycle and that improvement was bound to come. The much more important truth for Canada and the Minister of Finance is that all the indicators, both here and in the country to the south of us, show that 1963 will again see a downturn of economic activity. The duty of this government, as of any government under similar circumstances, is to plan our economy so that we can meet the situation which will arise next year.
All economic indicators have put up these danger signals about next year and, whatever the minister may say for political consumption, I have learned in my short sojourn here in this chamber to respect his intelligence enough to feel certain that he knows as well as I or anyone else, that there are danger signals ahead and that there will be difficult times which we will have to deal with when we come to the turn of the new year.
However, in order to make the picture even better than it is the minister engaged in a little bit of statistical sleight of hand. For

instance, he kept on comparing the figures for the second quarter of 1962 with those for the first quarter of 1961. I am sure he knows that is a thoroughly bad way to look at statistics and that it is utterly wrong to present such comparisons. I suppose he was on a search for little points of consolation, and again it would be mean to begrudge him that satisfaction, but I would like to point out what happens when he engages in that kind of comparison.
He informed us that the gross national product in the second quarter of 1962 was almost $4 billion higher than in the initial quarter of 1961. That is quite true; but if he had compared-as he should have done and as any economists advising him would have told him to do, if they did not in fact tell him-the second quarter of 1962 with the second quarter of 1961, he would have found that the increase was only $2.9 billion rather than the $4 billion he was talking about.
There are other similarly intriguing sleight of hand bits throughout the minister's presentation and the statistical comparisons which he made. Neither I nor the other members of this group are concerned with that kind of exercise, innocently and charmingly as it may have been carried out-at least charmingly.
The point we in this corner have been trying to make to this house and to our country is that Canada faces a long term problem of unemployment and the long term problem of evolving a program that will expand our economy to meet that unemployment. The point we have been trying to urge upon this house and the country is the need for a modern approach to the role of government in our society.
Look for a moment with me, Mr. Chairman, at the cuts in the revised estimates. Look at the $8.5 million cut in our contribution under the Colombo plan. This represents a 17 per cent cut out of the niggardly total of $50 million for this international aid program. I say to this committee, I hope not offensively, that this reduction is not only an act of meanness in a world which cries out for generosity, but it is also harmful domestically because our contributions to the Colombo plan, as the Minister of Finance well knows, are mainly made in goods and services. Therefore, this cut does not save us any foreign exchange, and is another little contribution to the slowing down of our economy in Canada.
Look at the savings in construction which go right through the revised estimates. Almost half the total reduction of $228 million is composed of reductions in capital expenditures; and about two thirds of that half are in construction programs. I had occasion to
Ways and Means
suggest the other day when first speaking to this house, and I repeat, that a first year economics student would have informed the minister and the government that construction programs are most important in an economy because of the multiplier effect they have in the jobs they create, right down the economy to the steelworkers, the cement workers, the brick workers and the plants involved therein; and because of the multiplier effect they have in the way in which the income distributed to the workers at one end is multiplied in the hands of a number of workers down the line. Yet the government at this stage, with the rate of unemployment we have and with the low rate of growth in the economy, does what is to me an incredible act of not only reducing the estimates but reducing them in the one sector where the effect on the economy would be worst. If anybody can suggest to me a more stupid approach to the program-and I use that word after hesitation, because I think it is the correct word-I would like to hear it.
I ask, Mr. Chairman, that you look at some of the other cuts; the cut in hospital construction by nearly $2J million; the cut in payments to and construction of hospitals for Indians and Eskimos by more than $1 million, or about 40 per cent. Again I say this is not only an act against the social conscience of the country, but it is also harmful to the economy for the reasons I have given.
If that was not enough, one was utterly flabbergasted on studying the reductions in the estimates to find cuts in capital expenditures in the Atlantic region, of all areas of Canada; cuts in transportation expenditures and in building estimates for a region where unemployment has been at its highest, a region which requires more and more job opportunities. Yet the minister deliberately takes government steps to cut the number of job opportunities there. And he is a Nova Scotian, as I was just reminded. I suppose that shows his even-handed way of dealing with Canada's problems.
The only thing that saves the reductions in the estimates from being an absolute disaster for Canada's economy is the fact that $228 million is a relatively small factor in the total of economic activity both public and private; but in principle, and when these cuts are taken in the context of the rest of the government's policy, disaster is not too strong a word to describe what is before this house at the present time.
Mr. Chairman, some of us in this corner of the house before we came to parliament- and some of us who have been in parliament for some years-have often been accused of being doctrinaire in our views about the

Ways and Means
economy. I want to say to hon. members through you, Mr. Chairman, if I may, that as I have listened to the major spokesmen of the two major parties in this house and read their speeches I have come to the conclusion, as I think any objective observer would, that they and not we are the real doctrinaires in this house.
Throughout their speeches you find a blind, illogical, traditional adherence to the private enterprise myth in our economy. It is a myth, because it does not exist; because the private enterprise sector is in the hands, for the most part, of large corporations; because the outstanding characteristic of our present economy is either monopoly or oligopoly. It is not the small, private entrepreneur who is of importance in our economy in 1962. Yet no speaker of the major parties on either side of the house has been able to suggest any planning where he will not immediately pull himself back, as did the hon. member for Davenport and say-I am not quoting him but this is, I am sure, not a misrepresentation of what he said-"I want you to understand that even though I stand for planning, I do not mean that there should be any public spending in competition with private enterprise. Nor do I mean that planning can be done any better by the public agencies." In fact, said he, "The best way of planning in our economy, when our economy works best, is where responsibility for economic decision is kept in private hands."
That kind of statement by an hon. member, if I may say so, who made an analysis of the economy of great value to hon. members of this house, could only be made by one who is so completely blinded by a doctrinaire approach to our economy as to be unable to see the avenues along which intelligent planning and intelligent direction must take us, perhaps blinded by his connections as well as by his theory.
Why don't you read the whole thing?

I read the whole thing. On the other hand, the group immediately opposite us are of course in a separate category. They have become not only blinded by doctrinaire orthodoxy; they have become the high priest of the worst in our economy and in our present system. I notice, for example, that some time ago the hon. member for Villeneuve, who is not here today, as he was not here yesterday-I wish I could have said it in his presence-was quoted as having said that Hitler is one of his political heroes.
I am glad you said "quoted".
It is in his words. Let not the hon. member run away from it.
I am glad you said "quoted".
That is right; and if the hon. member agrees that he was correctly quoted, that is what I am after. He was correctly quoted.
We do not agree.

The hon. member does not agree with the hon. member for Villeneuve; I am delighted to hear that. In fact I was certain there would be some members of the Social Credit party with a sufficient sense of democracy and real freedom to disagree with a statement as irresponsible as that.
You are twisting the words, sir.

I am not twisting the words. If the hon. member will wait he will hear my words, and I am sure he will see that I am not twisting them. The hon. member for Villeneuve was quoted in the French edition of Maclean's as having said Hitler is one of his political heroes. He later explained that what he meant was the economic policy pursued by the German government under Hitler during the 1930's, and not his political and dictatorial policies. I was interested to note in the Globe and Mail this morning, in a story about a meeting the hon. member for Villeneuve had at the University of Toronto yesterday, at the bottom of the front page, that someone asked him what were the economic policies of Hitler which he admired, and his answer was "I do not know what the economic theories were during Hitler's time in Germany".
I can only come to the conclusion that the hon. member for Villeneuve admired Hitler for his economic policies, about which he knew nothing. I say in all seriousness that this is an important key to the hon. member's mind; I regret he is not here. More particularly, it is a key to the hon. member's tongue, which is a great deal faster than the other part; and, perhaps, a key also to Social Credit theory as a whole, that you admire something about which you say you know nothing.
I respectfully submit, as does our party, that the approach of the government as well as that of the Liberal spokesmen will lead us into further difficulties. I suggest it is wrong to have private enterprise as a goal in itself, worthy in itself, just as it is wrong to have public enterprise as a goal in itself, worthy in itself.
That is what you did.
No. You can have both. The hon. member has never understood what we are advocating.
What about the Regina manifesto?

Oh, I could make a speech about the Regina manifesto and then, perhaps, the hon. gentleman would understand it a great deal better. If my words are not too presumptuous, I could also say something about Saskatchewan. However, if the hon. member does not mind, I propose to go on with the notes I have for my own speech.
I was saying it is wrong to have private enterprise as an end in itself, just as it is wrong to have public ownership as an end in itself. Both are means to an end. If I were asked to state the difference between views we in this corner hold and those of others in this chamber, I would state it in this way: at the present time in our economy, the major purpose of our economic activity is the profit of the industry involved, and social welfare is a hoped for by-product of that purpose. In my submission, that is standing society on its head. That is standing social morality on its end, destroying the social and ethical purpose of our community. What we require is a society where the major purpose of economic activity is social welfare, with private profit a hoped for by-product. If one turns the purpose around-
What was the purpose of the Liberal social program for 22 years?

The purpose of the Liberal program for 22 years was to stay in power; its purpose was to do enough to fool the Canadian electorate to elect them again. From the behaviour of hon. members opposite during this session I would think that the purpose of the Liberal party has not seen much change.
We suggest we must organize our economy so that the national welfare is its major purpose, and that in order to do this we must have an outlook which is as ready to tread on the toes of the big corporations as it is to tread on the toes of every other special interest-labour, farmers, lawyers and doctors; that there must be an approach to our economy which makes-and I use that word deliberately-the large corporations in the economy play a part in reaching the national goals and not a part only in making profit.
What would happen if they all moved out?

Well, they could not all move out. But if there is a government which has inventiveness, then what there is of capital resources in Canada belongs to the Canadian people, and there are ways and means of making sure that they remain at the service of the Canadian people. I suggest that no corporation has the right to move out of Canada merely because the Canadian parliament asks it to serve a certain purpose, any
Ways and Means
more than any individual would be morally right in taking that attitude against a democratic decision of the parliament of Canada.
Furthermore, I respectfully submit that such a thing would not happen, because if the plan which we have suggested in this parliament were followed we would have full employment in this country and a much bigger opportunity for reasonable profit and for economic development than this country has ever known. In such conditions there would be no reason for corporations to leave Canada. Furthermore, they have not done so in the past in any part of Canada, no matter what government has been in power, and they will not do so in the future despite what the hon. member suggests.
They did in Cuba.

That interjection, if it was heard by the reporter and goes on the record, is an indication of the kind of irresponsible political viciousness which I had hoped we had got rid of on our Canadian scene.
There are two or three points in what is before us which indicate the difference in approach to these questions. There are, for example, the tax incentives which were suggested as a means of stimulating private investment. That was also in the statement made by the spokesman for the Liberal party. May I point out, as did my hon. friend from Nanaimo some days ago, that we already have excess productive capacity in the country, and that we are not going to produce anything worth while by further tax incentives for investment, because the investment is not needed.
May I illustrate this by a couple of examples. In current dollars, business investment on new fixed capital fell from $7.3 billion in 1957 to $6.5 billion in 1961, a drop of 11 per cent. Over the same period total business reserves or savings grew from $4.9 billion to $5.1 billion, an increase of about 4 per cent. So that at the same time that private investment fell, the reserves available for investment actually increased. Thus there is no need for any further tax incentives; the reserves are there.
Let me indicate another point. In 1950 depreciation allowances accounted for about 72 per cent of total business savings. That is already a high figure. By 1961 depreciation allowances accounted for 85 per cent of business reserves. Despite this, the amount of net private investment fell in 1961.
The same kind of criticism can and should be made of the proposal to remit taxes for increased sales. The way in which this scheme is now presented to the house means, I suggest, that a situation could arise where businesses which increased their prices would get

Ways and Means
the benefit of this remission of taxes whereas businesses which decreased their prices would not derive any benefit. Obviously when you put the tax remission on the basis of the dollar value of sales, you could actually have a situation where a business which increased the volume of its output but decreased the price of the product, would come out without any increase in the total value of its sales and, therefore, would not benefit from the tax remission. Surely what you want is a volume increase and not a price increase in sales.
Similarly, it should be obvious to hon. members that if you remit taxes on the basis of the total increase in the value of the sales, you can easily have a mere transfer of sales within the economy without a total increase in the economy at all. In other words, you could have an increase in the sales by A at the expense of B with the total result exactly the same it was previously, but A would get a tax remission and the economy would not be one whit better off.
May I also remind hon. members, if they need reminding, that every time our economy expands, economists have found that, on the average, for every 1 per cent of expansion of the gross national product there is about 1J per cent of expansion in the national revenue. Hence your problem of deficits can only be solved, in my submission-as has been said many times from this corner-in terms of a growing national product, and of an expanding economy which will result in expanding revenues for the federal treasury.
In addition to other proposals which have been made we wish to suggest the following in place of those which are now before the House of Commons. We suggest that instead of an increase in the personal exemptions in the income tax system, there should be a direct cut in the tax for the lower incomes. That action will immediately stimulate the consumption demand which is what you require in the present economy. You have got to attack our economy much more from the consumption demand angle than from the investment angle. It is the lack of purchasing power which is your major problem at the present time. You will meet that objective by lowering taxes for the low income groups. The suggested increase in personal exemptions is obviously a regressive and not a progressive way of doing it, since the same increase in the exemption applies to a man who makes an income of $30,000, $40,000 or $50,000 a year as to a man who makes an income of only $3,000. It obviously means a great deal more in actual tax saving to the man in the higher tax bracket than it does to the man in the lowest tax bracket.
We say, second, as we have said on many occasions, that the way in which to deal with the recession threatening next year is to increase government spending instead of cutting it and to increase it on the building of social capital. The estimates which were revised by the Minister of Finance in our view should have been revised upwards instead of downwards. I am sure that some of the expenditures squeezed out by the minister were properly squeezed out. As is always the case with every administration of whatever party, whether government or private, it gets into the habit of putting a great deal of water in the expenditures which ought from time to time to be squeezed out. I am certain that has happened in Ottawa as it happens in every other place. But subject to that kind of saving, I urge that the estimates should have been up and not down so that we would have had enlarged estimates for the building of hospitals and schools, universities and parks, recreation centres and roads, low cost housing and slum clearance and urban redevelopment; the public development and conservation of natural resources in association with provinces; technological and scientific institutions in co-operation with the provincial governments.
I urge that we need the building of homes for the aged across Canada, and expanded geriatric services at one end of the age scale as well as child welfare services at the other end. We also need an increase in the social security program, particularly for old age pensions and the portable pensions which we suggest.
All of these things, as we have had cause to emphasize, require over-all national planing in co-operation with all the agencies of government and of economic importance in this country. Everybody is now for planning, Mr. Chairman. As a matter of fact, government spokesmen and Liberal spokesmen vie with each other as to which one of them thought of planning first. However, what I mean and what this party means is actual planning for the input and output of the economy, on a three year, four year or five year basis as is thought desirable for the length of a parliament. What we mean is a plan which will be worked out in consultation with the provinces and with all economic agencies-capital, labour, farmers and the like -so that it will have the most democratic basis possible and which would incorporate the social and political goals of our society: higher education; social welfare; full employment; full utilization of the capital equipment in the country which we have now, and the building of additional capital equipment in order to provide jobs for new hands for whom we shall have to provide work in the next while.

These must be placed in a plan, we submit, of which the budget forms a part, so that the fiscal and financial policies of the nation fit into the structure of the goals which we set for ourselves as a nation.
In that matter we must be concerned with the social and political goals first and with the economic ends and means next. I submit that we should not start, as I have said, with a preference for one kind of ownership or another, particularly when the economic history of this country has in fact shown that none of the social capital required, some of which I have indicated, will ever be filled adequately or at all by private capital, and that only public investment can possibly do the job.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member but I must inform him that his time has expired.
I am prepared to sit down now, Mr. Chairman, or to continue if the house will give me two or three minutes to complete my remarks.
Agreed.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is the committee agreed?
Agreed.

I particularly suggested two or three minutes because I wished to say something with the hon. member for Villeneuve here. I wished to say that the funds for this kind of development can be obtained both from monetary expansion through the Bank of Canada-
Hear, hear.
-and through borrowing from the chartered banks, if necessary.
Come and sit over here.
Not at all. I would have to lose a good many attributes which I value to sit beside the hon. gentleman in this house.
You have nothing to lose by leaving the socialists.

Let us not get into competition on that score. I was going to say in the presence of the hon. member for Villeneuve that the Social Credit party some time ago had a glimmer of truth in the fact that you could expand your money supply and thereby reduce the interest charges and place money in the hands of the consumers in order to absorb what the increased productive capacity has produced.

That is right. I will give you an answer.
Ways and Means
That glimmer of truth has so blinded them that they have been unable to see anything else ever since.
You are wrong there.

It is only a glimmer of truth, and it is only because they have been blinded that the hon. member for Villeneuve was able even for a moment to contemplate in a country like Canada agreeing with Dr. Hjalmar Schacht, the economist under Hitler, and feel proud to display a letter which he had from that servant of the most cruel dictatorship in the history of the world, rivalled only by Stalin of the Soviet union. To be proud to display a letter from the economist of that most cruel dictatorship is something which could occur only because the hon. member was so blinded by that little glimmer of truth concerning money in the hands of consumers. The fact is, Mr. Chairman, and I submit it as a fact, that in the economy what is important are the goods and services produced by men and women.
That is exactly what we have been saying.
You just listen a little longer and perhaps you will start talking sense.
You are just starting to talk sense.
And money is merely the measure of what is produced in goods and services-
Right.
-and certainly you must have the measure properly adjusted or you will get false ideas.
Right.
You are a Social Crediter. Come over on this side.
The hon. member is just showing that he does not even know anything about Social Credit when he suggests that.
We know you are a Social Crediter.

It is important that the measure should be adequate for the purpose and should be properly handled, and it is easy to upset the economy if the measure is not properly handled. But having a lot of money will not produce goods.
We never said that. You are saying that.

If, therefore, hon. members opposite mean merely enough money in the economy to meet the needs of the economy-

Ways and Means
Right.
At the right place.

-enough money in the economy in the hands of the consumers, and if they stop talking nonsense about the difference between national income and the gross national product, as the hon. member for Villeneuve incessantly and invariably does, then they do have hold of a glimmer of the truth. If to that they will add the concept of modern planning, the concept of intervention of the government in the modern sense, they will have another glimmer of the truth.
You were so good a moment ago.
Wait a minute. I will be even worse in a moment because the most significant statement by the hon. member for Villeneuve was made the other day on a bill before the house-
He is the best member in the house anyway.

Who is? Let it be noted, Mr. Chairman, that the member who said that the hon. member for Villeneuve is the best member of the house was the hon. member for Villeneuve.
I am saying, Mr. Chairman, that the most significant statement by him was made during the debate on a bill presented by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre proposing a minimum wage of $1.25 per hour. The hon. member for Villeneuve stood up in his place and in his rapid and charming way-
Thank you.
-said to the house at that time that he was in favour of a minimum wage.
He wanted not only $1.25 but $1.50 an hour.
Right.
And then in the most demagogic way conceivable he went on to tell the house that he was opposed to the intervention of the government to enforce a minimum wage.
Opposed to the controls.

I respectfully submit to the heckler, who has no respect for parliament by his presence as well as his absence, that that is demagogic irresponsibility.
(Translation) :

Mr. Chairman, on behalf of the voters of the riding I represent, may I say that I am pleased to take part in this discussion.
The people of the constituency of Compton-Frontenac are practically all farmers. As a matter of fact, it comprises two small towns, with populations of 8,000 and 5,000 people respectively. They constitute the two largest industrial centres in my riding, and that is why I said that I was representing a mainly rural population.
Mr. Chairman, the Canadian people want their moral and vital needs to be satisfied. Not only do these people want a decent way of life, but they also want the various social groups to be protected. They want each man to be respected as an individual and as a human being. They want the present system to be adjusted to moral values, and the basic natural law to apply to all men, which means that each and all of us should be respected.
In short, this new law means the continuation of life, the preservation of human life.
The setting up of this new world will take some time, and, perhaps, courage as well as perseverance, but it also may be quicker than people would imagine. That is the task of our generation. We have to rebuild on the ruins of the present system.
Mr. Chairman, the former governments, the luminaries of our universities, the professionals of our economic organization are responsible for the present situation. It was up to them to keep the world in peace and order. They did not do so. They did not keep those terms and we have to bear the consequences.
Moreover, the people are losing confidence in the philosophy and principles of our present system, because they are not in harmony with the Christian principles of decency and justice.
There is general discontent among the people. There can be found fear, insecurity and undeserved hardships. Hoards of essential goods are wasted and the pangs of hunger are felt by close to two thirds of the world population. This is an absurd and stupid situation. We face imperative needs which must be satisfied. Life is a perpetual creation where man is searching for and finding his own image. But if he is to live of the spirit, his vital and moral needs must be satisfied.
Material needs of men are easy to list: they are food, clothing, shelter, heat and sanitation.
It is a shame that thousands of people, both in Canada and throughout the world,

should suffer from hunger and cold. For this reason alone, our civilization stands irrevocably condemned. Proudly materialistic, it should at least meet the prime requirements of the people, but up to now, it has failed to do so.
In that respect there are undoubtedly in Canada some privileged citizens, namely those who control money and credit, those who manufacture guns, ships and planes. For them, the present system is a blessing.
But the people who foot the bill by supporting the heavy burden of debts, of taxes, in addition to all other unrepaid debts because of fantastic interest rates, cannot be satisfied. This situation cannot last. The world shall not know peace and rest as long as the natural aspirations of man are not satisfied.
That is why we must assume our responsibilities as a nation and as individuals if we want to get results in politics and in economics.
That is why the electors from Quebec decided to withdraw their confidence from the old political parties that are crippled with paralysis. The people who voted for our party chose to support a rejuvenated policy which will take into account the economic realities with regard to the needs of the population, a truly Canadian policy that Social Credit will bring to them.
That's right.

The old parties help the unfortunate of the world, but overlook the destitute of Canada. The old parties provide credit facilities to foreign countries, but restrict credit for Canadians, the builders of our country. The old parties know where to find money in wartime, but cannot provide a living for Canadians in peacetime. In wartime, plenty for all; in peacetime, misery in the midst of plenty. That is what the old line parties have given us.
Social Credit wants to master money and credit so that production may serve its purpose and help the people.
Money is intended to buy what is for sale; it must serve its purpose. This means that we should circulate as much money and credit as there are products and services available.
That is correct.

Social Credit wants to
master money and credit so that the human person may reach freely its full development.
Social Credit wants a balanced Canadian economy with a decent standard of living for one and all.
Ways and Means
Social Crediters want better family allowances and better pensions for old people as well as disabled people and the blind. We also want better allowances for veterans and needy people. All that without any tax increase. On the contrary, we want income tax exemptions to be raised to $5,000 for married people and to $3,000 for bachelors.
Social Credit wants to use the Bank of Canada for the development of our natural resources. We are in favour of using the Bank of Canada to finance the provinces, municipalities and school boards. The Bank of Canada should also help farmers and facilitate the construction of housing. Interest should be charged only to cover administration costs. There should not be any interest at fantastic rates, as is now the case, excessive interest allowed by the old line parties since confederation.
I listened carefully to the speech of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) when he stated that he would be able to restore the economy by all kinds of means if, naturally, he were in power. In reply, I ask the Leader of the Opposition: how is it that the moment your party is in the opposition you can solve everything, but when it was in power you could not do anything?
After the depression and the war, what did your party do during the 22 years it was in power? You were there at that time, hon. members opposite. You say the Tories have not done anything. Then what is the difference between Liberals in power for 22 years and Conservatives for five years?
The political parties have given this country the corrupt politics of yesterday which the people can no longer stand. We are engaged in a struggle of liberation from the financial dictatorship which has denied us the right to benefit from the wealth of our country and to use it as we see fit.
We realize that we are faced with two enemies: the career politician who speaks of hardship amidst abundance and hands over to his ally, the financier, the profits which come from exploiting the working people. This is terrible, a criminal set-up.
The day is bound to come when we shall have a government which will take over the creation of new money. The public knows too well nowadays what the banks are up to and the money and debt system will become less and less suited to the enormous progress

Ways and Means
which the people will enjoy, and this in the near future.
The potentialities and the economic development of our country have grown tremendously, while the system we have of running into debt has thrown us head first into an awful slump. All in all, the more progress there is, the more we are strangled by those who run us into debt.
No wonder we experience a fictitious prosperity in times of war and an economic slump when the slaughter is over. The Russians, Chinese and Congolese are not to blame for the hundreds of thousands of unemployed we have in this country.
Our governments are to blame because they did not face up to their responsibilities and set up a financial system to serve the people instead of an inhuman system where human beings are treated like animals.
If we accept scientific and technical developments in all fields, why not accept the same development in the area of public finance?
There will be more and more unemployed among Canadian workers if we refuse to recognize the priority of man over money. But if we recognize that priority, they will enjoy more and more leisure.
Automation should please man and assist him instead of driving him to that kind of insecurity which handicaps him in his own country.
Old political parties offer no solution when the only thing missing is money. Why send representatives to every country in the world to try and sell our goods which our own citizens would like to buy if they had the purchasing power at their disposal?
How can we make coherent suggestions to other countries when we can do nothing in our own country in order to give Canadians their share of the Canadian production?
The country was not developed by government nor by finance. Finance and government would not have achieved much alone; they needed the brains and the arms of our honest Canadian citizens for that job. And while all those pioneers and builders were at work, our governments allowed a few individuals to exploit us as the development went on.
We have a tremendous national debt which practically paralyses all our activities and which carries the germ of inflation and deflation accompanied by a host of undeserved

hardships imposed upon our citizens in the name of civilization and freedom, a freedom which our people have never known since confederation.
Our old political parties, once in power, become totally unable to cope with financial problems, so much so that we wonder if it is not a disability pension that we are paying our members instead of a parliamentary allowance as true representatives of the people.
But you know that such hardships do not result from the fact that Canada is unproductive or unable to produce more. You very well know that the lack of bread on a Canadian table is not due to a lack of wheat; it is simply a matter of money.
The producers of goods and services are doing a very good job. They would perform an even better one if they were not faced with money problems.
That is right.

If the producers of goods and services refused to produce, you would expose them to the people and you would take the necessary steps to force them to produce.
But when the money producers penalize the Canadian citizens, why, gentlemen of the government, do you not have even a word of reproach for them? You penalize the producers of goods who do a good job and you show respect for the masters of money who do not do theirs.
The production of goods requires effort and skill; the production of money requires only a decision, and it is money that is lacking.
Nevertheless, it is a crime for governments to let human beings remain in such hardship amidst an abundance that is there for everybody to enjoy.
Each woman or child who goes hungry, who suffers from the cold and each family that is ill-housed is a living accusation against you, the old parties, which do nothing to put an end to that tyranny.
It is time to establish a financial system at the service of Canadians instead of supporting a dishonest financial system that overlooks entirely the possibilities of the country.
The economic and political ills of society are blinding, but we have to determine their causes scientifically if we are to apply the appropriate remedy.
What is the aim of economic planning? Does it provide employment for all? Or does it rather aim at producing as much goods as possible, as many products and services, with the least effort possible?

Improved agricultural and industrial methods increase production, and often replace man by machines, especially since the first world war of 1914-18, to the extent that today organized society can produce enough useful goods to meet the vital needs of all mankind while progressively reducing the part played by human labour.
The people realize more and more the enormous production capacity of the industrial system; but the old political parties still believe that the goods men need must come from the work of all the population just as it was before the coming of modern machinery.
On the other hand, the same people learn and notice that millions of people live in the most abject poverty, that the natural right to marriage is thwarted, because the system is unable to distribute the great wealth which it is able to produce.
Yet, even though they acknowledge that the situation is absurd, even though they speak out against it, the old parties ignore the real cause of the people's misfortune. They hopelessly advocate useless and illegitimate reforms.
Indeed, those reforms, communism and socialism, are useless and illegitimate because they ignore man's natural rights. They are useless because they do not constitute a true remedy; they are not the proper solution and they will never remove the economic ailments of our society. Besides, the popes have condemned such doctrines and, for us Christians, that should be enough.
There are two distinct ways of achieving the aim of economic planning, which is to provide the consumers, men, women and children, with essential commodities and services:
(a)	By production, means of transportation included;
(b)	By the distribution of those products among the consumers.
The first of those means, production, is getting to be more and more efficient. Consequently, it is not at that level that we will find the present ailment of our economy.
It is the second process we must examine in that regard. It is distribution which is not up to the mark and which is now paralysed.
As money is the instrument of distribution, the means of exchange, it is the monetary system which does not play its role properly. It does not distribute the goods produced.
Ways and Means
Fundamentally, money plays the role of a ticket, it facilitates the exchange of goods, as our friends opposite were saying a while ago. The value or soundness of money is based on the people's confidence in their country's producing power.
The natural function of money is to ensure the continuous distribution of all the useful commodities which the people produce and need.
Today all governments have neglected their duty in surrendering control over the money system to a small group of men who do not give a hoot about the primary purpose of money and who have turned it to a use which is exactly the opposite to what it should be. Thus, those men have absolute economic and even political control over society.
The controlling power of our financial system today, that is the masters of the banking system have reserved the right to issue money; they create money and put it into circulation in the form of debts that must be refunded to them with interest. With the repayments they demand at fixed dates, they withdraw and cancel that money even before the products have reached the consumer.
Since money is the instrument used to convey commodities from producers to consumers, its withdrawal deprives the people of their power to purchase all the goods they have produced. The banking system, in withdrawing more money than it has issued, makes money scarce at a time when products are plentiful and workers ask nothing more than jobs.
Hence the exports and the unrestrained competition for foreign markets, because there is not enough money on the domestic market. Hence international indebtedness, economic conflicts leading to wars. Hence also a progressively increasing control over agriculture, industry, capital and the natural resources of society, a control which places the universe at the mercy of this world bank monopoly.
The banking system tries continually to withdraw as soon as possible the money issued for production, without bothering to see whether that money did also make distribution possible. Hence a number of disastrous consequences:
(a) A frantic competition in which efforts are made to reduce costs as much as possible by cutting salaries or by putting pressure on the workers; then efforts are made to sell at the highest price possible, in order to recover the total costs, including the interest on money "created out of nothing".

Ways and Means
Hence we see a continuous succession of bankruptcies. The weakest and the meekest are eliminated by competition because the consumers lack sufficient purchasing power.
We see an increasing accumulation of products which do not sell, despite the need of consumers who cannot afford them.
We are witnessing a progressive failure of that attempt, because machinery displaces workers and because the equipment so increased is soon idle, since the consumers lack the money to buy the production of that equipment.
Governments tried to correct such conditions through various palliatives, such as public works or financial assistance to the most stricken. Peter is robbed to pay Paul and poverty increases instead of being eradicated.
Governments have only two ways of raising the money they need for such remedies:
1.	Through taxes collected on the already inadequate income of the consumers;
2.	Through bank loans. New money created by the banks but later recalled, increased, because of the interest it bears.
The failure of such remedies is therefore most obvious, because they will leave the consumer burdened with a larger debt and more and more lacking in purchasing power.
To solve the problem, it is clear that the governments must reassume their prerogatives and themselves exercise a control over the money supply needed by the people.
The government must base the money supply on the productive capacity of the country, issue new money not as a debt to the banks and saddled with interest charges, but issue debt-free money.
To automatically prevent any risk of inflation and deflation, and to maintain a perfect and continued balance between prices and purchasing power, prices will have to be according to production and consumption statistics. Such discount shall be calculated to bridge the gap between prices and total purchasing power.
Is anyone opposed to Social Credit? Yes, and I will mention a few classes of opponents. The bank magnates and those of the trusts operating within orbital control of the banks are opposed, because they can sense the loss of their precious monopoly, of their means to exploit the public. Their political flunkies who are more sensible to the realities of the election funds than to the needs of the public back up the bankers' opposition.

Political parties have not yet incorporated Social Credit in their program, because they are listening to the voice of their financial backers and because the people, inadequately informed, have not yet raised their voice.
The 30 members in this corner of the house, who were elected by over 500,000 voters, are starting to inform the people of the province of Quebec and Canada.
Those in charge of the patronage are generally opposed to Social Credit, because if the public has some money, they will lose their importance.
Some people among the newly rich are opposed to Social Credit because they like to throw into the shade those who own very little. They fear that if the public does not need to crawl for its right to live, it will judge men on their moral worth, and not on their wallets.
I notice that our opponents state or deny but that they do not prove anything. Or if they do, they distort Social Credit in order to make it open to criticism, but one of them has gone as far in this house as to give a false interpretation to certain texts in order to introduce an unwarranted meaning in them; the name for that is not ignorance but deceit.
It was St. Louis, King of France who said:
The first duty of a king is to strike coin when there is not enough for the economical good of his subjects.
It is not at all necessary or even recommendable to do away with the banks or even to nationalize them. A banker is an expert in accounting and investment. He is therefore entitled to continue to receive and invest savings and to keep a part of the profit.
But printing money is an act of supreme authority which should not be associated with a bank. We must take the supreme authority away from the bank and give it back to the nation.
Ledger money is a good modern invention which must remain, but instead of originating from a private source, as a liability, the figures representing money must originate from a national agency, as a servant of the nation.
We must not tolerate-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. I regret to inform the hon. member that his time is up.
(Text):

Mr. Chairman, during the course of the last several weeks we in this comer of the house have attempted to put before hon. members of the house, for their

judicious consideration, certain recommendations and proposals that we sincerely believe are in the way of concrete assistance in relation to the two tremendous problems facing us in Canada today, namely an inadequate rate of economic growth and the major question of unemployment. On each occasion, from each opposition corner of this house, as if sitting on their white steeds and waving their banners in the air, we have heard the traditional cry of "socialism. These are the people who are going to destroy our freedoms." Mr. Chairman, this tactic and this approach is not at all dissimiliar from what we find in the John Birch society and similar ultraconservative and right wing organizations. Surely we can expect, from responsible representatives of the people, that they will attack us and criticize us positively and constructively, and not with false labels.
You don't even know what you are talking about.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Villeneuve rose in the house the other evening with, I believe, this very dictionary, the Concise Oxford dictionary, and read the definition of the word "socialism". I would like to point out to the committee, first of all, that we do not find any mention of social credit in this dictionary, and therefore we can assume that socialism is at least more significant, as far as these people are concerned, than social credit.
Just read about Christianity and you will find out about social credit.

Second, Mr. Chairman, I want to suggest to the hon. members opposite and other people who are attacking us on the basis of supposedly being socialists, that this is not, once again, a question of socialism versus free enterprise. Let us ask the question, first of all: is the program that is being promoted by the New Democratic party a program of socialism? We had it in the words of the hon. member for Villeneuve, and from the Concise Oxford dictionary here the other evening, that in a socialist state, the state or the government takes over and controls all the means of production and the resources in a society. We do not propose to put this particular program before the people. We do not propose to adopt these policies.
Then, Mr. Chairman, it is suggested in this particular definition that in a socialist society the rights and freedoms of the people of the nation are destroyed and taken away. Once again, this is not the objective of the New Democratic party. Rather to the contrary, we are interested in controlling the monopolistic tendency of the capitalist society and enlarging and expanding the scope of the free-
Ways and Means
dom of people; enlarging the freedom and opportunity of people to obtain for themselves adequate and decent housing and all the education which their children can take advantage of, regardless of their ability to pay.
If I might paraphrase Mr. Churchill, who I am sure is a much more acceptable reference in this house than either Hitler or Mussolini, Mr. Churchill once said, "Is a man any less free when he is adequately housed and adequately clothed?" This is the principle on which the New Democratic party is operating. We say, do not criticize us for what they say we are. Criticize us for what we say we are and for what we propose. We will accept your criticism on that basis.
Just what is the program of the New Democratic party? What, in brief, are we proposing when we talk about the problems of economic growth and unemployment in Canada? We say that a federal government, in relation to the capitalistic, industrial and automated society that we have today, must provide leadership. We say that a federal government must intervene in the economy in the interests, in so far as is necessary, of the common welfare of the citizens. We say that we would adopt intelligent but democratic economic policies.
How?

This is not classical socialism, Mr. Chairman; but if this is socialism, then I am a socialist and proud of it. We can cite as evidence of the value and the success to date of the types of measures which we have been recommending and which we will continue to recommend, the experience of the west European nations and, in particular, the nation of Sweden.
You don't know anything about Sweden.

Some time, when I have an hour or two, I will tell hon. members something about Sweden. But we must go back a few days to the remarks of the Minister of Labour in this house when, in an attempt to decry the value and success of democratic economic planning in western Europe, he said: Yes, it is true; it works; it has been successful; but, surely, you socialists are not going to recommend that we should adopt measures used by nations which pay lower scales of wages than the rates paid to Canadian workers?
This is another example of inaccurate and misleading Conservative statements. They continue to beg the question. They decline to stand up and document their answers. What do wage rates mean by themselves? They mean nothing. A wage rate has to be related to the cost of living in a country. The actual wage rate is not important. What is important is a low cost of unit production, and this is

Ways and Means
where we can compare the standards of west European democracies with those of Canada. Further, I would point out to the government and to the Minister of Labour that 74 per cent of the exports of the United States come from ten companies with the highest wage structure in that nation. Finally, 85 per cent of the imports which we took into Canada this year came from a country with a higher wage structure than our own. Surely this negates the argument used by the Minister of Labour.
What of free enterprise, which conservative-minded members opposite hold up for our admiration, even going so far as to invoke some of the papal encyclicals in their support? I have just as much right to discuss those encyclicals as they have, and I suggest to them that if they read "Rerum Novarum" and "Quadragesimo Anno" carefully they will find in them the most ringing condemnation of the capitalist system to be found anywhere. Further, if they read the latest encyclical, "Mater et Magistra", they will find outlined there exactly the type of program which we are proposing in the New Democratic party.
Unfortunately, some of the reactionary conservatives in the Liberal party are still trying to discuss economic problems within the framework of classical economics from the days of Adam Smith. They are a hundred years behind the times. Adam Smith defined economics as that science which deals with the allocation of scarce resources. That is not the problem of North American societies today. Our problem is not one of production. Our problem is one of distribution.
We do have important basic social and economic problems here in Canada. Certainly, we still have an unjust distribution of wealth. We can all agree on the desirability of increasing our production so that everybody can share in the increase. Even traditional thinkers on both sides of the house agree as to that. What is more basic and more important is the redistribution of the wealth we already have in this country.
We have an obligation to the developing nations of the world. Two thirds of the people of the world are not as well off as 85 per cent of the Canadian people. I suggest that this traditional Conservative blocking of change has to stop. We have to wake up. We can no longer afford to be complacent. In support of the argument I am trying to present-I have found it difficult because of the interruptions-let me point out that it is not only the New Democratic party which is suggesting we should introduce some fundamental change into our thinking and in our approach to the problems of industrial societies today. Let me quote briefly from a

publication issued by the centre for the study of democratic institutions. I am sure this is a publication of an organization which we can all respect. I quote:
Economic theories adequate to an industrial revolution are not good enough for the conditions of the scientific revolution. The complexity and interdependence of the scientific industrial state calls for national planning. Government must intervene more and more in the nation's industrial life.

He said: Mr. Speaker, as the title of this bill makes clear its purpose is to provide for statutory holidays with pay for workers in

Canada who come under federal labour jurisdiction. Let me make it clear, in view of things that have been said in other debates, that we recognize that that is as far as federal legislation can go. This bill goes no further than that. It relates only to employees who come under federal labour jurisdiction, but it provides that for such employees there shall be eight holidays during the year on which they shall have the day off and shall have it with their full pay. The days suggested in the bill are New Year's day, Good Friday, the 24th of May or whatever day near that is celebrated either as Victoria day or as the Queen's birthday, July 1, Labour day, Thanksgiving day, Remembrance day and Christmas day.
The principle of the bill is, I am sure, one that commends itself to members in all quarters of the house. All the parties represented here have pronounced themselves at various times in favour of workers having statutory holidays with pay. I hope, therefore, that the debate need not be lengthy and that the bill can be given second reading whereupon I would be happy to move that it be referred to the standing committee on industrial relations. By offering to have it referred to that committee I give the undertaking so far as I am concerned that details of the bill can, of course, be altered in the committee if the committee so wishes. In other words, what we are dealing with at this point is solely the principle of the bill which, as I say, is that there should be eight statutory holidays with pay and provision that when employees are required to work on any one of these statutory holidays they shall receive extra pay for such work.
There is not a great deal of legislation on the statute books of Canada providing for statutory holidays with pay. There is some to which I shall refer. This is in fact one of the reasons that I present this bill, in the hope that once again the federal parliament might give the lead, a lead that I would hope might be followed by provincial jurisdictions. There are actually only two provinces thus far, Manitoba and Saskatchewan, which have provisions of general application dealing with public or legal or statutory holidays. Most of the other provinces have some provisions, but they are restricted in that they either provide holidays for only certain elements of the working population or in that they provide for holidays but do not provide any pay for them. In the two provinces that I named, Manitoba and Saskatchewan, there are provisions for statutory holidays with pay for all workers, seven in the case of Manitoba and eight in the case of Saskatchewan.
I am happy to say, Mr. Speaker, that in terms of being specific the best piece of legislation that we have regarding statutory

holidays is the Civil Service Act, chapter 57 of the statutes of the federal parliament of 1960-61. Section 62 of the Civil Service Act provides as follows:
The following days are holidays for the civil service:
Then there are listed nine specific days which are holidays for the civil service and there are provisions which make it clear that these holidays are to be had with pay. Then there are provisions for regulations dealing with the question of either extra pay or compensatory time if persons are required to work on these particular holidays.
It will be noted that the Civil Service Act which I have in my hand spells out nine holidays whereas in my bill I am only asking for eight. I should like to see more, but getting started is better than having nothing at all. The ninth day that is provided in the Civil Service Act is Easter Monday. As hon. members know, this is a holiday that is not yet too general outside of the federal civil service and the banks. Therefore at this point I am actually asking for employees in Canada generally, those who come under federal labour jurisdiction, something which is a little less than the federal government has already provided for its own employees.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, this is something that all parties in the house are agreed upon. It is something that many people think is on the statute books but it is not there yet. Therefore we in this party feel that the time has come to put this kind of legislation on the statute books. I hope that the debate may be brief so that the bill can be given second reading. If that happens it is very clear that all the house will have done will be to approve the principle of the bill. If there are details in it that members feel should be altered I would be quite happy to have them altered in the committee on industrial relations, but I suggest that here again is an opportunity for the platforms of all four parties to be implemented by placing this piece of social and labour legislation on the statute books. I therefore move that second reading be given to Bill No. C-15 to provide for statutory holidays with pay.

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF STATUTORY HOLIDAYS WITH PAY FOR EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-15 is one that has been before us on many

occasions. I recall that during my first session in this honoured chamber the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) introduced a similar bill and we had at that time a very good discussion on it. Following that he became vice president of the Canadian Labour Congress and the former hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam re-introduced the bill in 1959 and again in 1961.
I was interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Nickel Belt following your remarks, sir, as to whether or not the bill was in order. The hon. member said he felt it did not require extra funds but I disagree with him in this regard in that the bill covers hourly rated employees and would necessarily involve extra funds.
The stated purpose of the bill is to regulate the terms under which employees in industries coming under federal jurisdiction may be employed on designated statutory holidays each year. It also provides that on any of the eight designated statutory holidays on which an employee does not work he is to be paid at his regular wage rate, and further, if he works then he is to be paid his regular daily wage plus two times that wage, making his pay three times his regular daily wage rate. As an example, if a man were paid $15 a day he would receive $45 a day if he worked on a statutory holiday.
Therefore the principle of the bill is apparently to guarantee that federal employees should be free from work without loss of income on the regular general holidays mentioned by the mover of the bill. This is demonstrated in the provision setting out that the regular wage rate would be paid on the designated statutory holidays not worked. However, there is a further principle embodied in the bill, that work itself should be discouraged on general holidays. This is clearly implied in the stipulation that the employer should be required to pay triple the regular daily wage rate to those employees whose services are required on the general holidays covered by the bill.
The application of these principles is not a simple matter in the industries that come under the jurisdiction of this parliament. Complications arise immediately with respect to the kinds of operations in which the bulk of federal jurisdiction industries are engaged, for by and large their operations are continuous. The services they render, by necessity, are required week in and week out, on general holidays and other days. In fact, some of the industries with which the government is concerned are required by law to operate continuously. In some instances, moreover, as in railways, buses, air transport, telephone, telegraph, radio and television operations
Industrial Relations
the greatest public demand for the services of these industries seems to fall on the general holidays specified in the bill. Therefore while the alleged purpose of the bill is to require industries to observe days of rest for their employees on statutory holidays, its chief effect would be to require the payment of a high premium rate, in fact triple the regular rate of wages, for work that as a matter of public accommodation and in the public interest must be performed on these general holidays.
Although the bill has application to federal employees, if it were passed I am sure industry would be expected to follow suit.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has drawn heavily on Saskatchewan legislation for his legislative inspiration. In reviewing provincial legislation on this matter it is not surprising, therefore, to find that Bill C-15 most closely resembles the legislative provisions for statutory holidays with pay in effect in that province. These provisions include the same designated holidays and the same required rate of holiday pay, namely, regular wages when an employee does not work on a holiday; but for work required on a holiday Bill C-15 goes even further than the Saskatchewan legislation. In such circumstances Bill C-15 requires payment of triple wages while the Saskatchewan legislation required double time and one half wages, or in hospitals, hotels, etc. where service is necessarily continuous, either double wages or regular time plus a day off with pay within four weeks. Bill C-15 makes no such distinction in treatment with regard to industries required to maintain continuous service to the public.
The only other province which deals in a general way with the question of pay on statutory holidays is Manitoba, and the Manitoba legislation deals only with pay for work performed on such days, and there are only seven such days stipulated in Manitoba. The total wage required to be paid for such work is one and one half times the regular wage rate. In certain necessarily continuous industries compensatory time off may be given instead.
I would point out also, Mr. Speaker, that neither of those provinces suggests as high a rate of pay as is suggested in Bill C-15, namely, triple pay. I may add that no other province has comparable legislation for paid statutory holidays, and it is also of interest that in the United States there is no legislation on statutory holidays at either the federal or state level that is comparable to the bill under discussion.
It is noteworthy too that neither the number of paid holidays, eight, nor the
1X00

Industrial Relations
minimum amount of the premium required by this bill are prevailing practices in either the federal jurisdiction industries or industry in general.
The most recent survey of the federal jurisdiction industries concerning the number of statutory holidays and the rates of pay for them, was conducted by the economics and research branch of the Department of Labour in April 1958. This survey showed that 40 per cent of the workers employed in industries under the jurisdiction of this parliament received seven days or less paid statutory holidays annually; 22 per cent received eight days; 26 per cent more than eight paid holidays, and 11 per cent received no paid statutory holidays.
Although it was possible in this survey to obtain data on the rates of pay for work on statutory holidays only for non-office employees, it was found for this group of workers that the dominant practice was to pay double time or less for work on designated statutory holidays. Seventy one per cent of the non-office employees surveyed were in this category. Less than 1 per cent of the non-office employees covered by the survey received triple time for work on statutory holidays, the rate of remuneration proposed in this bill.
Mr. Speaker, I think we should perhaps review some of the collective agreements which now exist in some industries. I would first mention the railway industry. An examination of collective agreements in the railway industry that are covered by this bill reveals that employees in the non-operating railway groups have seven paid statutory holidays, but that such employees must have 65 days cumulative service within a 12-month period to qualify. Where the employee works on the statutory holidays, he is paid double time wages.
On the other hand, agreements covering train and engine service employees do not recognize statutory holidays at all, presumably because work performed on holidays by the road operating employees cannot be eliminated or minimized and the requirement of continuous operation is recognized as one of the elements of service. In other words, that is part of the job; it is part of the particular service provided by that industry, in fact, in railway passenger service the public may require on holidays more than the normal amount of weekday train services. This comment would probably also apply to air passenger and other transportation activities.
A provision for statutory holiday pay in shipping operations also presents special

problems which do not lend themselves easily to legislative regulation such as is proposed in this bill.
The Shipping Federation of Canada, which is an association representing deep sea steamship and stevedoring companies loading and discharging ocean vessels at Canadian Atlantic ports, St. Lawrence river ports, and certain ports in the great lakes, negotiates, on behalf of its members, collective labour agreements covering the hourly paid shore labour workers employed at such ports. The Shipping Federation of Canada has this to say:
Due to the peculiar nature of shore labour employment, longshoremen and other shore workers may be employed on any given day of the year, including Sundays and statutory holidays. You are no doubt aware that stevedoring work is casual employment and fluctuates widely during the season of navigation at Montreal and other ports in the St. Lawrence river system, and also over the 12 months period at Canadian Atlantic ports.
The collective labour agreements provide that double time is payable for any work performed on certain holidays. The holidays in question are, of necessity, different at Montreal and other ports which are not open throughout the winter months, and ports like Halifax and Saint John which operate all the year round. The double time holidays stipulated in the collective agreements are a matter of collective bargaining between the shore labour unions concerned and the employing steamship and stevedoring companies at each port.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, in the light of these circumstances which are peculiar to the stevedoring industry, if Bill No. C-15 were passed I am sure it would create hardship in that particular type of operation. According to another study made by the economics and research branch concerning holiday conditions provided in a sample of 835 current collective agreements covering close to 600,000 workers in Canadian manufacturing and non-manufacturing industries in 1957, only 6 per cent of the employees covered by the survey were paid triple wages where work was performed on paid statutory holidays. This, however, is the minimum rate required to be paid under Bill No. C-15. Thirty eight per cent were paid double time and one half wages, and 29 per cent double time wages for work on statutory holidays. None of the people covered by the survey received rates of pay as high as this bill proposes.
The survey also revealed, Mr. Speaker, that eight paid statutory holidays was the most common number provided for in collective agreements in manufacturing and non-manufacturing industries. About two fifths of the agreements included in the study, covering a like portion of workers, provide such a clause, whereas one fifth of the workers covered by

the study receive more than eight holidays. Almost two fifths received less than eight paid holidays.
If the proposals contained in this bill are designed to establish minimum standards of pay for work done on statutory holidays, it is clearly evident that the standard proposed goes beyond the minimum wage rates and the prevailing practice for holiday work established by collective bargaining in Canada. In fact, the wage rate proposed in the bill as the minimum rate to be paid appears to be the equivalent of the highest rates in effect in collective agreements, and these rates apply to only a small percentage of employees in industry in Canada. The effect of the legislation, if enacted, would be to establish, as a floor or minimum rate for work done on statutory holidays, a rate of pay which is substantially the ceiling rate thus far established in a very limited number of industries in the course of collective bargaining in Canada.
A major objection to this bill appears to be the failure to recognize or draw any grounds of distinction in treatment in the matter of pay for work on statutory holidays as between activities classed as continuous service operations and other types of operation. In choosing to enter this type of employment, workers should have a full recognition of the nature of the industry in which they are taking service.
There is another fact, Mr. Speaker, that I think we must keep in mind. I mentioned this on a previous occasion when this bill was before the house. I said at that time that another fact which enters into the picture is this. If one is to be paid three days' pay for one day's work, the mercenary angle may become more important than the holiday angle; the value of statutory holidays may become secondary, and the mercenary angle foremost. Therefore I think there are many aspects of this bill which we must look at before passing it. I would be the first to agree that it should go before the committee on industrial relations. However, in view of all these aspects to which we must give serious consideration and which I have tried to outline, it is obvious that the bill is open to serious question on several grounds. Therefore I would suggest that it should be rejected by the house for the time being.

Mr. Chairman, earlier this evening, in response to the allegation that the program and policies of the New Democratic party constitute communism, I had begun to cite authoritative and objective evidence which supports our ideas of increased leadership on the part of federal or central governments in the economic affairs of nations and more specifically in support of our idea of democratic economic planning. As hon. members will recall, I referred first of all to the centre for the study of democratic institutions sponsored by the fund for the republic of the United States and indicated that they had reached the conclusion that the complexity and interdependence of the scientific industrial state calls for national planning.
Second, in answer to the distorted interpretation of hon. members opposite, who seem to be very prone to quoting various encyclicals, I should like to read into the record the official statement of "Mater et Magistra" with regard to the role of governments in modern industrial society. I quote as follows:
Indeed, as is easily perceived, recent developments of science and technology provide additional reasons why, to a greater extent than heretofore, it is within the power of public authorities to reduce imbalances, whether these be between various sectors of economic life, or between different regions of the same nation, or even between different peoples of the world as a whole. These same developments make it possible to keep fluctuations in the economy within bounds, and to provide effective measures for avoiding mass unemployment. Consequently, it is requested again and again of public authorities responsible for the common good, that they intervene in a wide variety of economic affairs, and that, in a more extensive and organized way than heretofore, they adapt institutions, tasks, means, and procedures to this end.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, as evidence of support of the position of the New Democratic party, I would refer to the Lincoln formula which suggests that the function of government is to do for the people that which needs to be done, but what they cannot do for themselves or cannot do so well.
No, Mr. Chairman; socialism is not the issue. Socialism is a false issue. Its supporters can be seen to hide behind a false label because they cannot in a positive and constructive manner criticize what we propose. We do not propose, as would be proposed by a socialistic society, that public ownership take over the means of production in society. We do not propose that the individual should be subordinated to the welfare of the state. We do not propose the abolition of private

property. We propose that society be regulated so that the individual can really grow and develop his full potentials and make his contribution to society.
The real issue in this conflict is the issue of our attitude toward change. The real issue is whether we are going to try to find new methods and new techniques by means of which to handle the new situation in the modern scientific industrial state or rather society, or whether we are going to cling tenaciously, on the basis of tradition, to our old concepts which are no longer adequate. We no longer have a society in which we find scarce resources. We no longer have tremendous and abject poverty, in general, in our North American society. The problem today is not one of production. We have plentiful resources; we have an affluent society. Our problem is one of distribution and one of grappling and coping with the swift scientific advances being made in society.
But, Mr. Chairman, we admit that it is difficult to face up to the question of change. We in this corner agree that there is in man a tendency to cling to the old ways of doing things. There is fear of experimenting with the new. Fortunately for us, however, we are not obliged to experiment. The experience is behind us. The sound democracies of the nations of western Europe have proved that democratic economic planning can provide a desirable and good standard of living for people while at the same time maintaining their sense of dignity and their freedoms.
Change is difficult; but if we appear to be anti-change while our opponents are prochange, we enter into competition for the minds and the hearts of people with a hopeless handicap. We must be prepared to change our methods on two accounts. Internationally the uncommitted developing nations of the world need our financial assistance. They are looking to us and are investigating our techniques and our methods in order to see whether democracy is the answer; and the choice precisely is between democracy on the one hand and communism on the other. I suggest to you that in western Europe again, the western European democracies, precisely because they have adopted democratic economic planning, are refuting the need for the existence of this philosophy of communism; and in these countries there is no danger of a communist doctrine taking over. But second, Mr. Chairman, and perhaps more to the point, domestically we are approaching a type of economy in which there simply will not be enough jobs of the traditional kind to go around. If we are not prepared to cope with 27507-3-71
