this problem a social and political crisis will be the result.
Planning has generally been accepted in Canada today, even among some elements of the chamber of commerce, and I daresay that the New Democratic party is to a great extent responsible for legitimizing this word and this idea. There is a difference, however, between the ideas there are in this house with regard to planning. I am not going to discuss the planning ideas of the Social Credit party because it seems to me that their philosophy is that, that government is best which does not govern at all. I am not going to talk about the attitude toward planning of the Conservative party because I am afraid that with their traditional Conservative approach to problems they are not prepared to make the changes necessary to adopt this idea of democratic planning.
This leaves us then with the Liberals who seem to have agreed with us that planning is a good thing; but once again, unfortunately, we must point out that the Liberal association with planning represents the adoption of a word rather than the acceptance of an idea. For example, I should like to quote for the record an official statement made by the planning expert for the Liberal party, Mitchell Sharp, when he said:
Nothing in my experience leads me to believe that the decisions of any group of public servants, however able, could or should be substituted for the decisions made by businessmen competing freely in the marketplace.
This statement can be found in the Toronto Star of January 12, 1962. This is precisely why the planning program of the Liberal party is not the answer. They say that it must be left up to private enterprise but we know that private enterprise is interested solely and entirely in their own personal profits. This is their reason for existence. We say as opposed to this that we must democratically plan and control the affairs of the nation in the interests of the common good. Our planning is precisely democratic because we say that we would set up a planning board which would be responsible to cabinet, which in turn would be responsible to the House of Commons. Nothing is more democratic than this part of our program. Planning is indispensable, I suggest, if we are going to make sense out of our future in this nation.
I wonder whether the hon. gentleman would permit a question?

When I have concluded, Mr. Chairman. If we are going to face up to the tremendous implications of the new trading patterns that are developing around the world we have to accept democratic planning. If we

Ways and Means
are going to provide for a faster rate of economic growth we must plan how we are going to develop our resources and in what direction.
I would go so far as to suggest that we have two choices before us in Canada. There is either going to be economic union and eventually political union with the United States, or else we can maintain our political independence by adopting the democratic economic planning of the western European nations and then taking advantage of the tremendous new trading opportunities which will be open to us as a result of President Kennedy's trading legislation.
So I suggest that the time is ripe for doing away with phony verbalism. Let us get on with the job of building Canada. For those willing to admit that free enterprise is not a divine dispensation and capitalism not a dictate of some natural law, the need and, indeed, the tremendous value of democratic economic planning to man and his future is everywhere evident. It is imperative in these times to revive respect for law and government as the proper institutions of the general welfare. Without such understanding the economic future of this nation of ours will be determined, warped and, indeed, undermined by the accidents of private ambition and the hope of private gain.

Mr. Chairman, as this is my maiden speech in this house, I am very happy, like those who have already spoken, to congratulate you on your election to the responsible office you occupy and I wish to assure you of our co-operation in the discharge of your difficult and important duties.
I listened with earnest interest to the hon. members who have taken part in this debate. Mr. Chairman, I feel a great deal of sympathy toward many of them. There is absolutely no doubt about their sincerity, but they keep wandering in the maze of outdated economic theories, which no longer meet the needs of a modern administration.
Whatever certain members or certain political parties may think, the main problem facing us is one of economics and finance. This problem is so important and is so diversified in its aspects that it almost discourages any initiative and consequently becomes obstacle No. 1 to any true expansion. Whatever the level attained, whether municipal, provincial or federal, the result is a wandering in a maze of dead end avenues.

I have much regard, Mr. Chairman, for all scientists and economists, but with all due respect for their knowledge and culture, I believe the time has come for them to learn that the period of trials and errors has now passed and that their period of experimentations has served to show this country their lack of competence, or even worse their deliberate maliciousness.
This session is now entering its second month, and my colleagues in this house, one after the other, both my honourable friends opposite and my honourable friends to my right, have mustered the full implement of their rhetoric and talent to prove the tottering of our country's economy and the absolute necessity of putting the tiller hard over in order to give new impetus to our economy toward a peak, and to enable Canadians to adequately play their parts in all walks of life.
The money-debt system necessarily results in interests, and interests, in their turn, true offsprings of a diabolic financial system, result in general taxes and income tax. We can see very clearly, Mr. Chairman, that our governments need some money for the administration of the nation. But what we do not agree to-and that is why we are in this house-is the excessively heavy burden of these general taxes and income tax, which paralyses private industry and slows down our economic development.
What we are fighting is a system which goes against the sacred rights of the individual and deprives him of part of his freedom. We are constantly progressing towards a system where the individual will be replaced by a number, and will be robbed of his individuality in the process, for in that system the human being will be of secondary importance, and the individual will be a mere cog in a huge piece of machinery called public administration.
We are proud to belong to a democratic government, it actually is the best we can have; but for goodness sake, let us not, in the name of that democracy which is dear to us, play into the hands of our enemy by killing personal initiative with systematic planning.
If our country now occupies a privileged position among nations, if Canada, thanks to the constant labour of its citizens, has managed to develop its immense possibilities, it is thanks to the full and complete freedom of action which has presided over its destinies.
Our financial problem is complex. Those who are now in control of money and credit are powerful, and they want to maintain their hold. Our money system is basically

unsound. The basic institutions in our whole economic structure are worried and they should be.
All classes of society are alarmed. Our debts are increasing all the time, interest rates are climbing and represent a far too high proportion of our budgets. Figures have already been quoted, which I do not think necessary to repeat. What answer do we have to all the questions that are being asked?
Every member of this house has received a mandate from his electors. Each and every one of us has a strict and specific duty to perform. Each member of the house, whatever his political affiliation, is formally committed to his fellow citizens and the country as a whole. We should, at this stage of the debate, fully and squarely face the problems before us.
The group to which I am proud to belong is suggesting as a remedy to our precarious situation a complete reform of our monetary system. "Utopia", some economists will say; and politicians talk about "funny money". Now, Mr. Chairman, it seems that as a result of our active presence here, certain persons who, until today, systematically refused to study our doctrine, have already begun to do so, and we are especially happy to note that many members are also studying, in an objective way, the Social Credit principles we stand for. I should like to quote a sentence from Claudel which makes very much sense when you think about it:
The truth of a proposition has nothing to do with the number of people who reject or accept it.
We realize, Mr. Chairman, that the full and immediate application of our principles would create a rather difficult situation in this country, but we are convinced, because we want to be honest with our electors and with the Canadian people, that the time has now come to start reforming our monetary system and to pursue that reform gradually, as circumstances and the country's requirements will allow.
We urge that positive and effective action be taken immediately to enable every Canadian citizen to develop freely in his own chosen field of activity, according to his needs and to his natural disposition. We want to warn the government that we do not intend to prostitute our movement and that if they keep ignoring our just claims, we shall have no alternative but to make it for them, as for any responsible government, a matter of life and death.

Ways and Means
Unemployment is a social evil that we must fight. I am a labourer myself, a union member and also the mayor of a small town with a labour population in a proportion of 95 per cent and I am familiar with the concern and great distress of that important social class. The first measure that we advocate is the establishment by the government of a municipal development bank whose role would be to provide to municipalities, without interest or rather at administration cost, in conjunction with provincial authorities and with due respect for their autonomy, the necessary funds to enable them to realize the public utility projects that the whole population so badly needs.
Those measures will serve a double purpose; they will put an end to unemployment, a real social evil, and solve the most urgent problems of the municipalities. Waterworks, sewers, sidewalks, street lighting, public park developments and many other projects are waiting, precisely because our municipal corporations lack the required funds.
Let me recall an experience I had as mayor of my village. During 1961, the municipal corporation of which I have the privilege of being the head carried out waterworks projects for about $200,000. Well, Mr. Chairman, because of our interest bearing money-debt system, my fellow citizens will have to pay $520,000 for a $200,000 service. In my opinion, that is a situation which has been going on for too long and which must be corrected at all costs.
The winter works program has certainly been a welcome experiment and the minister responsible for it deserves our commendation. But, to my way of thinking, that is nothing but a pain-killing poultice and not the effective cure for a much more deeply rooted disease.
Mr. Chairman, so long as we do not strike at the root of the evil, and the real cause of the hideous evil of unemployment which has marked our age is not readily recognized, we shall keep going round in circles and we shall never come out of it.
At the risk of incurring the wrath of the eager profit seekers, I say that one of the best solutions open to us is the setting up of that municipal development bank and I venture to point out to hon. members of the government that if they want to survive the present crisis, it is a must for them to listen to us and take really effective measures to fight unemployment.

Ways and Means
Mr. Chairman, 1 have a formal undertaking with my fellow citizens and workers and I am not going to bargain with government authorities on that matter. We, Canadian citizens, are first class citizens and we insist that our rights be respected, including the right to live a real life in the fullest meaning of that word.
We owe a great deal to our business executives and I admit it, but we also owe very much to the working class of our country which has shared to a large extent in the development of our resources. Through fair legislation, we want to create within the Canadian nation a climate of understanding between management and labour, which will enable the Canadian nation as a whole to benefit from the begt elements on both sides.
I noticed, with dismay, that considerable cuts had been made in the estimates of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fulton). Having a special interest in that matter, my constituents are worried by the cuts made in connection with this important department. In view of the fact that they do a large share of the construction work of the federal government, the stone and granite workers are worried and wondering what the future has in store for them. For a few years now, the chief public works architect seems to have a particular taste for imported materials. Let me remind you at this point-and I am not afraid to call myself an expert on that subject-that in Canada, in the province of Quebec particularly, and especially at Saint Marc des Carrieres, he will find the stone which will meet the requirements of the Canadian climate and the basic rules of architecture.
Our products are good, our workers are experts in their trade. Let us show them confidence and show foreign visitors that Canada has not only good materials but also expert workers who are capable of making the best possible use of that stone.
As the member for a constituency only a quarter of which is inhabited, I am sure I will be allowed to expound here a project which is particularly dear to our hearts, the development of roads to resources.
The riding of Portneuf, which has been blessed by divine Providence, with enchanting and truly exceptional sites, has remained forgotten and anonymous because of this lack of roads.
We are in urgent need of highways which would serve as links between Quebec city and Lake St. John, Quebec city and the northern reaches of the province, Baie Comeau and the whole Abitibi region. Such highways would certainly be an efficient contribution to that decentralization of industry we need so much and they would also open access to resources, up to now undreamed of.
All these steps, Mr. Chairman, can only be implemented by putting at the disposal of the provincial administrations considerable amounts or, which would be even better, by giving them back what the federal government gradually took away from them during the war.
Canada being the result of co-operation of the provinces, the most important thing is first of all to respect their rights.
Our farmers are hard up and unable to sell their products at prices which would allow them to operate their farms. We hear justified complaints about farm desertion and the exodus toward the cities, of the younger generation especially. But, Mr. Chairman, these young people who leave the farms do not want to be considered as second class citizens any more when they see their fathers work from sunrise to sunset without managing to provide their families with the minimum of comfort and welfare which they are entitled to.
It is no use flattering the farmers at election time and telling them what a noble and worthy profession they have. What farmers want is the right to live on the plot of land of their forefathers, the right to remain there as masters and the right to help their sons start out and live in the neighbourhood of the family farm. That is what our farmers want and what they are entitled to. We will succeed in that only if our agricultural products find markets at prices which are fair and reasonable.
It is not logic, Mr. Chairman, that our farmers should have to mortgage their farms to have the right to live on them. Farm credit certainly plays a large part in our economy, but let us not forget that the success of the Farm Credit Act depends directly on the need in which our farmers find themselves now because for too long, unfortunately, our farm legislation has been improvised by politicians rather than directed by true legislators familiar with the problems of our farmers.
Mr. Chairman, we deplore once more the deficit of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Nowlan) which amounts to approximately

$500 million. That is a new argument in favour of our monetary theory.
We dare our hon. friends not to increase the burden of taxes which will soon amount to 50 per cent of the value of our products. They realize that the people's needs are ever increasing. So they try to find excuses and they come up with one deficit after the other, or five in as many years.
Mr. Chairman, the moment of truth has almost come. We shall no longer tolerate the pursuance of an ostrich policy, and the situation will have to be faced. Last week, the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire), in a brilliant statement of our principles, put forward many suggestions. We know very well that however logical they may be, the measures he advocated will be ignored by this house, but for goodness sake, let the government suggest at least something new. Let them propose new solutions, since the ones submitted in the past have brought on the failure we are experiencing today.
What we advocate is the control of money through the Bank of Canada. Money which is meant to facilitate the exchange of goods has become a heartless and ruthless master demanding slavery.
Let us put things in order and let us, through an imaginative legislation, give the consumer the purchasing power he requires. Then, only, will we restore the lost balance and will we, at last, see our Canadians give their full measure and fulfil their mission in the world with dignity.

Mr. Chairman, although I had the opportunity of making two or three very brief interventions in the debates thus far, this is the first opportunity I have had to deal in detail with some of those problems which I feel are of vital importance to us. This opportunity not only gives me the privilege of mentioning some of our major national problems but also the privilege of bringing to the attention of the committee some of the situations which exist on a more or less local level.
During the debate to date the shortcomings of the government have been pointed out in great detail. I believe the present administration missed one of the greatest opportunities
Ways and Means
ever presented to any government in any country and in any age when, having an overwhelming majority in the last parliament, it could have promoted and implemented new and dynamic policies that would have placed Canada at the top of the list and proven beyond any question the potentiality of a free democratic society.
Instead of that what did it do? Instead of moving forward in these positive ways it began to perpetuate the follies of the Liberal administration. The members of the government lost the vision and they settled back into mediocrity.
I remember the former Liberal prime minister making a statement after his defeat in 1957 that the people voted for a change but all they got was a change of faces. I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, that actually there is not very much basic difference between the Liberals and the Conservatives.
References were made during the course of this debate to the tight money policy of the present government. It was brought to our attention by the hon. member for Davenport. It is true that under the present administration we have tight money; but remember, Mr. Chairman, we have had it in the past, we still have it, and to all appearances we are going to have it for some time to come. But I would remind the committee that during debates several years ago, when I had the opportunity of being here, I heard the Conservative members loudly berate the Liberals for their tight money policy. In fact up in my office I still have a sheaf of papers, clippings and documents pointing out the serious effect of the tight money policy instituted by the Liberals on the various segments of our economy. Therefore when the hon. member for Davenport says a vote for the Conservative party is a vote for tight money I would suggest that, apparently in this particular respect at any rate, there is not very much to choose between the Liberals and the Conservatives.
The hon. member for Davenport also spoke about high taxation. He said a vote for the Conservatives would be a vote for high taxation. Well, Mr. Chairman, I have a very interesting document in my possession. -we believe that a major reason for the serious trade situation is that we are being taxed out of the markets of the world by unnecessarily high
taxation.

He went on to say:
I believe the entire tax structure in Canada needs to be overhauled with a view to providing encouragement to the promotion of primary and secondary industries in our country.
So we find here again that apparently there is not too much difference between the Liberals and Conservatives, because they both believe in tight money; they both believe in high taxes. Then we find that under fire, what do they do? They point out similar actions taken by the others when they were in office and give that as a reason for warranting their pursuing the same policies. The Liberals apparently are greatly concerned about the members of the Social Credit party in this house. In fact, Mr. Chairman, it seems they have appointed their hatchet men. I refer mainly to the hon. member for Laurier. It seems to be his mission to try and annihilate the Social Credit party, perhaps with the intention of trying to whip Quebec back into the Liberal vote. But I would suggest that his frustration is clearly obvious. I think he had better do just a little more homework and do it more thoroughly, or his reputation as a Liberal brain may suffer some serious setbacks.
Last evening the hon. member for Laurier made some reference to Social Credit. By the way, Mr. Chairman, there have been a number of references to Social Credit and once or twice I have been on the verge of complimenting some of the hon. members for studying Social Credit. However, I exercised a little restraint and did not do it, and now I am glad I did not because I find that afterwards they indicated very clearly and conclusively that they just do not know what they are talking about when they talk about Social Credit. Last evening the hon. member for Laurier quoted from a document which was numbered 7-62. I have a copy of that bulletin here, Mr. Chairman; it is information bulletin 7-62.
Where did you get it?
That would be interesting. We have it on file, you know.
Tell us where you got it.

Anyway, the committee will remember that the hon. member for Laurier referred to that particular document, reading from another one, and inferred that it was an official publication of the Social Credit Association of Canada. I would like to repudiate that this evening, because it is absolutely false. If the hon. member had read the last part of this particular document which I have here, he would have seen it makes this statement, that this secretariat- which he was quoting-has no connection

with any political party. I would suggest that the hon. member for Laurier was shooting in the dark, or else there was some other motive behind his reference to that document. It is unfortunate that the hon. member is not in his seat this evening. No doubt he has other responsibilities. I do not like talking about an hon. member or referring to him when he is not in the house, but I felt this was the only opportunity I would have in this connection.
The Liberals are trumpeting loudly about the glory that would accrue to the Canadian nation if they were in office. I would remind them that they had 25 years to prove that.
We did.
We did; that is why you are still alive.

Perhaps, Mr. Chairman, these initial remarks might be interpreted as being political. If that is so, I would like to change the picture and go along to dealing with a number of matters which I feel are of vital importance. We believe very strongly that there should be set up a department of dominion-provincial relations. Some would say that we already have enough departments in this government. Some would say that we already have too many. They would also suggest that adding another would only result in a duplication of activities and interests. However, I strongly believe that if Canada is to remain strong and united within the framework of our constitution, close and careful attention must be given to the development and maintenance of a mutuality of confidence and co-operation between the national government and the respective provincial administrations. I believe the best way to accomplish this objective would be to have a special department with a full time minister who would take care of this particular aspect of our national and provincial activity and give his full attention to it.
I know that the problems and issues that could be handled by such a department are many and varied, but I would like to refer to just a few this evening to point up what I have in mind. Some references have been made by hon. members of this particular group to the setting up of a municipal development bank. I would suggest this is one of the most pressing needs of our country at the present time. Adequate capital at the lowest rates of interest should be provided for use in non-productive projects. We would also suggest that this bank, the municipal development bank, would be an agency of the Bank of Canada. I believe this is a vital need in our economy today.
I should like to read an excerpt from a statement made on November 8, 1960 by the

Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities to the government of Canada.
The high cost of municipal capital borrowing continues to harass municipal governments. The prevailing situation is no different than it was a year ago when the federation pointed out that, unless the cost of money can be reduced to within the capacity of municipalities to afford, there could develop a serious setback to the progressive effort which municipal governments have been making in an endeavour to at least keep pace with their minimum growth requirements.
I should like to quote further, Mr. Chairman, but I believe that points out what I have in mind. Therefore, we have the need of municipal governments requiring to provide for their people the facilities and services at their particular level. The need is there. But we also say there is a tremendous possibility involved here, if we had a municipal development bank set up from which money could be provided, at the cost of administration, for use in the construction of vital projects such as hospitals, schools and other facilities in the public service.
As the leader of this group, the hon. member from Red Deer, pointed out, by the time the cost of such projects is repaid, it amounts to over twice the original cost of the project. Therefore we ask this question: why should this be so, when the facilities of the Bank of Canada can be used to provide this capital? May I also say, Mr. Chairman, that if this method were used it would ease the crushing burden on the municipalities and would enable them in turn to either increase the required services to the people or on the other hand reduce the rate of taxation. We believe, again, that if this method of providing social capital were used it would also leave private capital for investment in productive enterprises.
I took a clipping from the Montreal Gazette of this morning, October 30. In the very first paragraph of this article I read:
The Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities raised yesterday the question of making home owners' municipal taxes deductible for federal income tax purposes.
Then it goes on:
-the federation concentrated mainly on a long standing proposal for a national municipal loan fund, otherwise known as a municipal development bank.
It seems that if this particular facility were provided it would be a tremendous boon to the municipalities in meeting the costs of services for their people. I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, that this is one of the things that could be under the supervision of a department such as I have mentioned, a department of dominion-provincial relations.
I should like to refer to another aspect of the financial situation. I believe the time has
Ways and Means
long passed when we should have addressed ourselves to a reallocation of the tax dollar. Serious attempts must be made to provide for a more equitable allocation of the tax dollar as between the three levels of government. Though charged with the responsibility for providing the greater share of services, the municipalities and provinces receive only a minor share of tax revenues. Then, as the trend towards centralization continues in government, we find an ever increasing tendency on the part of the government to invade fields which really belong to the other levels of the administration. I think it is clear that the present formula is far from satisfactory. We remember the answer which was given by the Prime Minister to the pleas made for a more equitable division on the grounds that provincial and municipal governments were unable to meet their obligations. The reply was, in effect, that if they did not have enough money they should go back and tax the people some more. This was from a government which during the 1957 election campaign had complained bitterly about Liberal policy in this respect and promised a revision of the whole taxation structure. Five years has elapsed, and only now has a commission been appointed to look into this question. If I remember correctly, the Associate Minister of National Defence said this matter was going to be considered immediately. Well, five years have gone by, and I think it ought to be considered immediately if our policy is to meet the need. This, too, is a matter which could be taken under advisement by such a department as I have suggested.
I should like to refer to two or three projects which mainly have to do with the province from which I come. The first of these affects us seriously, as well as in addition affecting the whole economy of Canada. I would refer to the Columbia river project. I do not intend to deal with this subject tonight to any great extent, but I am confident that had we a department of dominion-provincial relations there would have been no need for the unpleasant and confusing situation which has developed over this great program. There have been many discussions, many debates, many articles written on this subject in papers across the country. There have been representations and misrepresentations. I feel that if there had been a department charged with the responsibility for dominion-provincial relations, retained a great deal more co-operation and such a situation could have been worked out on a harmonious basis and we would have respect between the dominion and the provincial administrations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do agree with the hon. member who has just sat down that there are many issues with which we are concerned and that we have many opportunities to discuss them. I do not know what the leader of the house has in mind, but I would expect that, possibly early next week, we shall have a motion to go into supply. There will be various other opportunities for us to debate these matters.
We have now spent six days engaged in a general discussion. Monday and Tuesday of this week have gone by, and there were Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday of last week. We shall have to spend a day or two at least dealing with the detailed resolutions. Of course, I am in the hands of the committee, but I would hope that if it were agreeable to hon. members we might go ahead now with the detailed discussion of the resolutions before us and leave the general discussion of economic matters, which, as I say, has now gone on for six days, to other occasions. I assume there will be many of them. Certainly, next week there will be one. when we could carry on this general discussion on subjects of interest to hon. members.
We have had a high level of debate. I think the level has been very high. I do not wish to curtail the rights of any hon. member; indeed, I could not do so even if I wanted to, because this is an unlimited debate. But the government has to get these resolutions through or, at least, it should do so, in order that the income tax legislation may be completed and returns filed before the end of the year. This is vitally important to many individual taxpayers throughout the country. If it is agreeable to the committee, I should like the committee to move now to the income tax resolutions. As was suggested by the hon. member who has just resumed his place, there will be other opportunities to deal with many of the questions which have been raised so far. If that course is not agreeable, then I reserve the right to speak later on, but I think in all circumstances the general debate could now be concluded.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I think those who sit on this side are in full agreement with what the minister said. There has, I believe, been a full and complete debate. I, too, would not wish to create the impression that we in the official opposition want to curtail the discussion in the slightest degree, but in order to substantiate what has been said I can only add that we have been waiting for this for the greater part of the day; for some time we have refrained from putting speakers up to

discuss the general statement which the minister made. Of course there are members who are ready and willing to speak but they too have felt, along with us, that the time has arrived when we might well leave the general debate and enter into a discussion of the detailed resolutions. So far as we are concerned, we would be prepared to meet the suggestion made by the minister.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?
Mr. Chairman, it is very difficult for us not to give way to pleas of such a charming person as the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the apology is accepted.

In so far as we are concerned, we have two more speakers and we do not feel that their remarks will take any disproportionate share of the time of the house. I must say that it almost embarrasses me to go ahead when I realize the sacrifice that is being made by the Liberals across the way. Last week I read with interest that the troika, the three key members of their front bench, had been called in to the leader's office, according to a report in the Globe and Mail, and had been asked to restrain themselves in order to give the men in the back benches a greater opportunity to speak. Here it seems that not only is the front bench willing to sacrifice but so is the back bench. I can only compliment them on this situation.
For the general good.

When the minister introduced this debate amongst his lead remarks were these very pleasant ones as found at page 795 of Hansard:
The Canadian economy has been expanding. Employment has been increasing and unemployment is decreasing. Our exchange position, Mr. Chairman, is improving and prices have remained relatively stable. The present performance of the economy is impressive by many standards.
That came to a good level of optimism. Later on before he sat down as found at page 808 of Hansard, he uttered these words:
Mr. Chairman, without any vainglorious boasting whatsoever, I simply say as a simple matter of fact and place it on the record from the figures which I put before the committee this afternoon and this evening, that the statements made by my colleague and myself in recent months with respect to the economic situation in this country have been entirely justified and that we Canadians are living in the most prosperous year in Canada's history.
I should hope I can say this with some vehemence. After repetition of this modest appraisal of the Canadian economy let me go on. Later on the minister said this as found
Ways and Means
at page 809 of Hansard. He is referring to these measures. He is talking about measures that need to be taken:
These measures must have two basic objectives. First, they must put Canada in a position to export substantially more goods and services to other countries. Second, they must put Canada in a position to produce more of its own requirements on a fully competitive basis. Our approach to achieving more economic growth and solving the balance of payments problem is expansive, not restrictive.
I read these remarks, Mr. Chairman, in order to point out that the new Minister of Finance is optimistic. We have had the most prosperous year in Canadian history. In other words things look fairly good and there are plans for the future.
I now wish to go on, Mr. Chairman, to deal with what was an experience of mine in the last parliament and many members who are in this one did not share that experience. I followed closely the performance of that government from the time it came in here with that surging crowd of hopeful, eager, gay faces, back after the election of 1958. They surged right around this room and almost pushed us out of that far corner of the chamber down there. They were here in all their glory for those years. I had the opportunity to watch them closely. I shared a room along the same corridor with many of them. I listened to their hopes, their deams and their aspirations as they all dovetailed in to support the great vision which had brought them here.
From them I gathered a bit of material. Many of these people, I suppose advised by their national headquarters, kept in touch with their constituents. I have here a collection of material. For example, here is a very nice letter sent out by the former member for Burnaby-Richmond. And when I read this letter I find that it begins in this way, "Dear friends in Burnaby-Richmond". It then goes on to tell of all the marvellous things that had been achieved, quite in keeping with what the Minister of Finance said at the start of this debate. I am almost saddened to note that the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond is not here. Then I have here a wonderful letter. It is from Dave Walker, former member of parliament for Rosedale. This letter just went out last fall. It is a very friendly letter, as one would expect from the former member for Rosedale. These are some of the things that he said:
There has been a noteworthy improvement in the employment situation; more housing and low rental accommodation are being built; the winter works program is being extended; huge technical and vocational training programs are under way; and exports are increasing. At the United Nations,

Ways and Means
Canada is a world leader In the campaign to end nuclear bomb testing and in the study of the nuclear fallout hazard.
Details about these and other important matters, which I trust you will read and think about, are on the back of this letter. I hope also that you will write me your views and let me know whether there is anything I can do for you personally.
Then he goes on to give a few intimate details about how he is trying to serve Rose-dale.
And where is he now?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: We certainly elected a great many more members than you did.

The hon. member for Saskatoon has interrupted me with a certain amount of vehemence. Would he give me the opportunity to go further in setting out the record of his government? He must admit that I am quoting from legitimate sources. I gathered such things as this, "Prime Minister Scores Again in Great Commons Speech". This literature went out in hundreds of thousands of copies and I managed to get one. Here are some of the things it said:
University grants doubled over 1957 level.
Second P.C. increase In old age, blind, disability pensions.
Exports up.
Farm income hits new high.
Employment production exports.
Exports up.
Production at new peak.
Help for Canadian magazines.
Free speech buttressed.
Canada tired of Liberal attitude.
Expansion accelerates.
Mining, gas show increases.
Predicts G.N.P. rise of 7.3 per cent.
Another waterway project.
Another $40 million acreage payment.
Steps to increase trade.
And so on. Then we have this document entitled, "The Record Speaks". I may say that it fits right into the modesty with which the Minister of Finance introduced this debate. I hope some of the new members who have not seen this pamphlet will take the opportunity to get it. I will lend them my copy. "The Record Speaks" has on the front of it one of these modest quotations rather in keeping with the general mood of that parliament; I refer to the last one. It states as follows:
The government of Prime Minister John Diefen-baker has accomplished more for the ordinary man and woman of Canada than any government in our history.
Mr. Chairman, not long ago in committee I made some remarks about the Liberal party and I did not get anywhere near finished with them. When I had told this to one of my Liberal friends he said this: "I would not go on if I were you. You will get the reputation of being an anti-Liberal or a pro-Conservative". From this applause which I have

received I judge that this is altogether likely to happen. I suppose hon. members can keep me drowned out to the end of my speech. I hope they will let me go on in fairness quoting from the record here so that at last I can give my own interpretation of it.
"The Record Speaks", which has this magnificent quotation on the front, was followed by some other pamphlets that show typical restraint-"Still More Action For Canada And Canadians", and "Four Years Of Action For Canada And Canadians". In them you get words such as these: "The greatest advances in social justice in Canadian history have been made by the government of Prime Minister John Diefenbaker," and "the greatest and most imaginative program of national development in the history of Canada is under way".
And so it goes. This is the kind of record that we have. I have here a publication called "The Conservative Canadian". It is, I think, an attempt-I hate to say this-to copy "The Canadian Liberal". This publication goes into the record. This is the kind of article that we have here: "Meet Canada's Newest Supersalesman". Then there is a picture and a flattering article about the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
All these quotations and examples I have given would lead one to believe, as my friends' applause would indicate, that everything is for the best in the best of all possible worlds, that this government has had this marvellous, stupendous record, that things were never better than they are today and this is the most prosperous year in Canadian history. I suppose there are people who accept this view; but the point I want to touch on and what I want to turn to is that somewhere in the midst of all that confidence that was breathed by all the 208 who came down here with their vision and their great leader, something went wrong. Colloquially something went haywire. We had an election last June and if the government of the Prime Minister accomplished more for the ordinary men and women of Canada than any government in history it is inconceivable that they should have been at least partially rejected at the polls last June.
If this record was the truthful case one would expect that there would have been some kind of triumph. Instead we have the Conservatives here with a minority government. I should like to suggest that there are a number of reasons why this took place despite all these marvellous actions. Despite the wonderful level of the economy about which the Minister of Finance has talked, somehow the Canadian people did not get the message or got a different kind of message

and partially rejected the government. I think there are some explanations for this. From the record I have read, with all its hyperbole and exaggeration in claims, I think it is evident that this itself is one of the reasons why so many Canadian voters turned from the government at the last election. I think the Conservatives managed to convince a great many people that they were doing a tremendous amount of bragging. Many of the things that they may have been able to present to the people as being things that they were proud of were missed by the very exaggeration of their political approach.
I have tried to understand as thoroughly as I can what really happened to this tremendous support that was there in 1958 and which melted away and left us with a minority government. I have come down to what I think are four key failings of the government and I would begin with what I think is maybe an over-all failing and one that relates to the Prime Minister. The new senator from Pickering, for whom I have a great admiration, in his first speech in the other place elaborated on the theme that there had been too many personal attacks on the Prime Minister. I think it is very easy to get carried away in partisanship and say nasty things about the other people, and I should like to point out to any members of the house who feel I am indulging too much in this that I probably said more flattering things about the Prime Minister in the house in the last parliament than any other member on the opposition side. I thought that he showed prospects when he came to power of being some kind of prairie Lincoln, but I have been very much disappointed. In my opinion, despite the best intentions in the world, he has let the country down and I think it is time that he should be replaced. I hope that the testing of the people is not too long delayed because, whatever my own fortunes may be, I feel that Canada very badly needs a new prime minister.
In trying to appreciate the failings of the government I come down to something that I think the Prime Minister himself failed completely to do, to establish a basis of trust with his own administrators and his own administration. I believe that the key here is that he tended to have an antagonism toward the administrators that he was left with and yet at the same time he did not have the drive or, if one wants to put it this way, the courage to dismiss a number of them so that he could at least feel that he was surrounded by people who were loyal to him.
The second aspect of the Prime Minister in his relation to the administration that I tend
Ways and Means
to find in noting his performance is that he has a very strong suspicion of expertise or the intellectuals or academics, whatever you want to call it. From all that I can gather from watching him and reading his speeches, he really does not want to trust what one might call the experts in problems in depth and, as I have pointed out before, this has had at least one unfortunate consequence. I have been to most of the universities in Canada and I find, for example that most of the academics and eggheads of the country in these places, who I believe have their contribution to make-I know that President Kennedy has found that they have-are supporters of either the Liberal party or the New Democratic party. I can count on one hand the number of academics, especially those of any real ability, who are openly supporters of the Conservative party or who have ever been in touch with any thinkers, including the Prime Minister, that the party may have. That is one vital weakness.
It seems to me that another aspect where the Prime Minister's approach has been weak is with regard to corporate business, and I think the appointment of the senator from Bay street underlines this. The Prime Minister has had a profound distrust of the business community in Canada and as a consequence has never tried to tap or really get in touch with the abilities that lie within the corporate structure of Canada. Hon. members may have had a different reaction but in my view the majority of the people engaged in corporate business in Canada whom I have scratched have tended almost invariably, ever since 1959, to talk Liberal or about what a great man C. D. Howe was.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that this is one of the fundamental reasons why the government, despite the glowing record of their performance which they put forward, was rejected by the people, because their leader was unable to compromise and work with the people in the administration, in the business community and amongst the brains, if you want, in Canada who have a great deal to contribute to the development of policies that are going to make our country great. Having said this, I should like to emphasize that I have no criticism of either the Prime Minister's good intentions or those of any other member of the house or of the government. But there has been a failure, and I point out to the members of the government that failure is no more apparent than in this glowing record that I have quoted or in the glowing remarks of the Minister of Finance when he introduced this

Ways and Means
debate, and then in what happened last June and what is likely to happen in the next election.
One of the points, Mr. Chairman, upon which I have always tended to agree with that columnist and writer in the Toronto Globe and Mail, George Bain, is what he calls Bain's law of political performance. This profound statement goes like this: The inclination of politicians to the performance of actions clearly having widespread public support increases in directly opposite proportions to the distance at which they stand from the next general election. This law, of course, is applying most strongly right at the present time, because I think all of us are aware that we stand imminently close to a general election. I agree with the law in that sense, and I think one of the consequences of the imminence is that politicians are likely to behave in a way to appeal to as wide a public support as possible. I feel that this is what all of us in this chamber are trying to do. One of the consequences, it seems to me, is that we may get a resolution out of this discussion, because we are so conscious of the next election, that will give the people a better opportunity to choose what kind of policies and what party they want.
In this connection, I would suggest to the minister and the government that it is time they gave over the long record of what I hate to call boasting, but it really is this, the long record of boasting that is indicated in most of their party propaganda superlatives in which they indulge, and acknowledge one of the realities of the last election, that they were partially rejected. Then, they should give to us and to the country a more precise, more realistic policy than they have in the throne debate that we have had or in the present budget resolution.
One of the great problems that I encounter in my own constituency is in the field of transportation. I have been here five years. We have talked and talked about freight rates and new railway policies, but we still have not reached any conclusion. We have not made a significant change that I have seen.
In the five years that I have been here, I have heard a great deal of talk about education and educational development, yet we are no closer to a national educational policy than we were before. There are no indicators in the throne speech, nor have there been subsequently, that we are moving towards it. When I first came down here there were many grave doubts as to the way the unemployment insurance fund was being handled. Later, there developed a rim on that fund that jeopardized the whole actuarial principle that was in it originally. Yet, we have had

no action, no indication really as to what kind of action we will have. This has been a live issue for a good number of years. We finally have something new, the so-called Neddy, the nickname that has developed in England for the national economic development board. Here, we have had no real explanation from anyone identified with the government as to what the scope of this board will be. It is very easy for any government member to point out that you cannot reveal this before the measure is introduced.
This is not so. This government has a record of having a spokesman put up a trial balloon; he gives a general outline of the way they are going to go. I recall the former minister of justice did this in connection with his censorship or obscenity law or the change in the censorship regulations. We have had no real indication, even though parliament has been going for five or six weeks, of how the government intends to proceed in connection with this national economic development board. It seems to me that this government is tending to perpetuate the very same tactics that were so disastrous to it in the last parliament. I would plead with them that what the country needs, even though some of us in other parties may not want it, is some real frankness about the legislative policies of the future, about where the government is going.
I should like to suggest to them that if this is not forthcoming, then the record of their party at the next election will be even more disastrous than in the last. They will be out again in the wilderness for years as they were before. All the indications that we have had so far are that they will go on projecting the same kind of record as was available in their propaganda record before. This is really going the way of disaster. If they go on with this line, they will go down. I do not think I am expressing anything other than my own individual views when I say that, whether one is a Conservative, Liberal, New Democrat or Social Crediter, this will be one of the great, sad things in Canadian history, that a party could come surging in here with the greatest approval any party ever had, any leader ever had, and dissipate it in five short years. I think that is the situation.
Now, Mr. Chairman, other spokesmen for our party have touched today on the planning that is the touchstone of the policy of our party. However, before I close I wanted to say how pleasant it was to hear the members of parties, my own and others, talking about their party philosophy, principles and ideas. It seems to me we need more of this. One of the things for which I am still waiting, of course, in this house relates to the hon.

members who represent the Social Credit party. They are very good at charging us and charging the people of Canada with not understanding or not knowing Social Credit. Well, how about telling us about it here? I think, Mr. Chairman, that if they really have something to tell, if they have a code or an answer, I should like to see them put it on the record.
You have the proof of it.

The hon. member says we have the proof. What I say is that you have to do some more teaching because I still do not understand. I am reminded of the Pat and Mike story, and I think most members have heard it, which explains Social Credit. Pat and Mike both went into business on the same day selling beer. They each had one keg of beer. Business was pretty slow, and they were right across the street from each other. However, Pat happened to have a dime and Mike did not. After a while, Pat got thirsty, went over to Mike, gave him the dime and said, "Could I have a glass of beer?" He had it and it tasted pretty good. He went back and the next thing Mike was over with the dime and he bought a glass of beer from Pat. Then, they went back and forth and managed to achieve total consumption with the expenditure of only one dime. This was a most illuminating story, and apparently it was used in the early days when Social Credit was on the sawdust trail in Alberta to explain these theories. I will agree that in a closed system, this worked perfectly. However, I want the story expanded so I can appreciate it in a fuller society. I should like it to be expanded to Pat and Mike, John and Bill and so on, so that we could see how it could really cover everything. I would hope the hon. member for Villeneuve would take the opportunity some time to elaborate on that Pat and Mike theorem for me. Now, one of the points that is bothering me most in trying to understand the Social Credit argument-and I would ask them to explain it to me-is that they are creatures of completely free enterprise and they adumbrate a society in which a bunch of wonderful small entrepreneurs are buzzing around and giving that society go, fervour and rise. This is their ideal. I have found most small businessmen are in a sense idealistic about themselves and they respond to this idea. But I want to ask the members of the Social Credit party how they are going to do something for the small businessman, the small entrepreneur, without greater government intervention, support and subsidies.
Ways and Means
By giving more money to the consumers.
How can they do this without restricting those elements which control so much of our society in its economic sense? How are they going to do it without restricting them?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member but his time has expired.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to delay the house too long. I shall not be more than a few minutes. If some members from this end of the house want to have the floor again, it is because of the unfair apportionment of speaking time as between members at the beginning of the session. A Social Credit member is given the floor for every ten members of the house.
True.

Mr. Chairman, I am not surprised to see the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) supporting the suggestion of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Nowlan) that the debate be closed because in his speech, last night, he made all sorts of promises and there is none left for any other member of his party who would like to take the floor now.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to associate with all the members who have offered you their congratulations on your election to the office of chairman of the committees of the house. The task that you assume is not an easy one and it includes great responsibilities, especially when the house is composed of a minority government and three opposition parties, one of which holds the balance of power, that is Social Credit. However, Mr. Chairman, you discharge your duties with efficiency as we all know.
Mr. Chairman, the government brought to the attention of the house its revised estimates.
Incidentally, I should like to thank and congratulate the Minister of Finance, because we received this afternoon the French translation of the revised estimates for the year 1962-63.
This is something new.

We notice that the Minister of Finance announces a reduction of about $233,394,305 from the previous estimates, in order to balance those of 1962-63. Out of this amount of more than $233 million, we notice a decrease of $30,076,443 for the estimates for the public works department.

Ways and Means
I realize it is not easy to balance a budget, especially with the monetary system we have at present. I am not an expert in accounting or in figures and that is why I wonder if the cuts that have been made are logical.
In my opinion, the Department of Public Works is one of the most important governmental departments since it has a direct influence on the economic development of the country and of each county in particular. Our counties are more prosperous when the Minister of Public Works has sufficient appropriations to meet their needs.
As for the riding of Montmagny-L'Islet that I am proud to represent in the house, especially since it was long represented by the former minister of northern affairs and national resources, Hon. Jean Lesage, who is now premier of the province of Quebec-
Only until next November 14.
God knows how much my riding has been neglected all those years.
It was not, but it will be from now on.

That is what you think. That riding, having been ignored for so long now needs the Department of Public Works. I mention, among other things, the construction of several post office buildings and particularly that of St. Jean-Port Joli. But the most important project is the blasting of the rock range off the wharf of Montmagny. That obstruction has been there in the riding for many years and was in existence under the Liberal regime, at which time requests were made many times to have it removed.
The blasting of that rock range would permit year round coastal navigation. That would have the effect of promoting the international tourist industry because, as every one knows, Montmagny has the finest hunting and fishing club on the whole south shore. That would also enable all manufacturers in the area to load the goods they are shipping on the north shore, or to some other place, directly in their locality. In addition, lumber companies could load their lumber directly at the Montmagny wharf, which, on the whole, would represent a substantial reduction in transportation costs. Many other companies or industries would surely be interested in establishing themselves in our area if water shipping was adequate.

There is also the human side of this problem which could be solved. We all know that lie aux Grues is part of Montmagny-L'lslet county. We also know that this island is inhabited by farmers upon whom rests our very survival. Yet, when they cross over to Montmagny to sell their products, these people often have to pay for an overnight stay and to wait for the next day's high tide before heading back home.
Mr. Chairman, I was also told that this spring a child in lie aux Grues, having suddenly taken sick, had to stay four hours on the wharf waiting for the high tide to be carried to the hospital. In the twentieth century, that is inhuman and unacceptable.
Mr. Chairman, even if the dynamiting of that chain of rocks should solve only the latter problem, the government must take the necessary steps to do it. The dynamiting of that chain of rocks would also allow the sand to disappear with the low tide and make navigation steadily possible at low tide.
Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the reductions made at the Department of Public Works were justified, and I shall explain.
Expenses in that department have been reduced by more than $30 million but they certainly did not forget to grant subsidies to crown corporations, to the prejudice, I suggest, of private enterprises. Therefore those subsidies are unfair, and I want to talk here of the subsidies granted to the C.N.R. In 1961, the Canadian National Railways received more than $81 million in subsidies. Those subsidies, enabled them to reduce their freight rates. The subsidies for 1962 will perhaps amount to $100 or $110 million. On top of that, the federal government makes up for the C.N.R. deficits. For each of the last two years, those deficits probably exceeded $60 or $75 million.
Almost at the very time the last railway subsidy was announced, the C.N.R. reduced their competitive rates below those charged by trucking companies on a wide variety of goods.
Truck owners do not receive any subsidy, either directly or indirectly. By paying high registration and licence fees, as well as heavy taxes on gas, they contribute their fair share to the cost of building and maintaining the roads they use. Since they undermine the basis itself of the competition between railway companies and other means of transportation, railway subsidies inflict heavy and increasing losses not only to truck owners and

to workers and suppliers in the trucking business, but also, and this is even more important, to all the Canadian people who, through their taxes, pay those subsidies to the C.N.R.
There are also those large grants the government is paying the C.B.C., another crown company. If those grants would all come back to our Canadian people, it might not be so bad, and would be rather normal. But, those amounts are partly used to bring French, American and other artists to Canada and, in many cases, to produce films in France which the C.B.C. needs for its local programs, whereas some of our Canadian artists are working for a ridiculous salary, when they are not starving.
Mr. Chairman, there is only one means to remedy all those problems, and it is that the government recaptures control of our currency. Nobody need tell me: "So we did," because it is untrue. Allow me to quote a text published in the Edmonton Journal on November 5, 1959:
In Shawinigan, the Minister of Finance, the Hon. Donald Fleming, stated that the Bank of Canada was independent of Canada and that it could not be ordered to increase or decrease the monetary fund. Mr. Fleming, speaking at a convention of the businessmen's union of Mauricia, added:
I insist upon the fact that the government of Canada has no power nor control with regard to the monetary fund. It may neither increase nor decrease it, and he added that he sometimes received letters asking him why he dealt with the currency reserve as if he was opening or shutting a tap. The truth is, said Mr. Fleming, that the Minister of Finance cannot in the least control the monetary fund.
Mr. Chairman, this is the main objective of the Social Credit, that is to reinstate control of our own currency before it is too late.
Our friends of the Liberal party-and more particularly the hon. member for Laurier-who are criticizing the Social Credit monetary policy to such an extent, would do better to go back a few years and recall that their former leader, who was then prime minister of Canada, the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King, when commenting on his recent victory in October 1935, said:
The result of the election is a sanction of the views of the Liberal party, that credit is a public matter of concern not only to the bankers, but to each and every citizen. Our victory is a verdict against the national bank owned and controlled by private interests, and a verdict in favour of a
Ways and Means
national bank well established to take care of rediscounting and of the control of money in terms of public necessities. Let there be no misunderstanding about it: this victory is a formal request for a return to government control of credit and money.
Mr. Chairman, during the great depression, the chancellor of the exchequer in the British House of Commons, Mr. Winston Churchill, made the following statement:
I am very serious when I state that this monetary convulsion has reached a point where I am convinced that the producers of new wealth will not tolerate indefinitely such an odious oppression.
I could also quote the words of Lord Beaverbrook, particularly well known in Canada, owner of several newspapers, who has been engaged in banking in the past, when he criticized the monetary system in April 1932. In the following article, we find, among other things:
Our monetary policy should have been reformed a long time ago. The needs of this nation require a constant expansion of credit facilities. The bank is the obstacle which stands in the way, and through the rights acquired a long time ago it has imposed a deflationary policy for the last ten years. The government must be the master in its own house. The government must dictate the monetary policy of the nation, and the bank should be put in its proper place, as a servant of the nation. Give us the right to establish reasonable credit and you will achieve adequate salary scales, price stability in commodities and prosperity for our people.
Mr. Chairman, those words were not those of Social Crediters but of Liberals of that day. The Liberal party though in power for 22 years, did not accept any of those recommendations. It merely rested on its laurels. I would therefore advise the present Conservative government not to do the same thing, to wake up, because at the next federal election, which will perhaps take place sooner than the hon. members think, the Canadian people, which is not asleep, will elect a government which will really take its responsibilities, and that government will be nothing less than a Social Credit government.
Mr. Chairman, all the governments in the world are seeking means to restore enduring peace. It is astonishing to see to what extent, all over the world, men are waging war in the name of peace. Peace, independence, freedom, happiness are at the basis of all the bloody horrors we hear about. Through power and terror we want to make man happy. What a poor and illogical concept of happiness. The only way to restore enduring peace in the

Ways and Means
world is to give each and everyone complete security and total freedom. And it is in that direction that all members, regardless of their political affiliation, should work, hand in hand, in order to achieve that purpose as quickly as possible.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, a moment ago I indicated to the Minister of Finance that we on this side of the house were prepared to accept the proposal made by the minister. It was, of course, on the understanding that we could come to a termination of the debate within a reasonable time. I see that is not possible; I understand there are hon. members from the far left who are going to speak, or want to speak, and others as well. Therefore, under those circumstances I would ask you, Mr. Chairman, to be good enough to recognize our side of the house and to see the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Brant-Haldimand.

Mr. Chairman, first may I offer my congratulations to the hon. member for York South for his engaging and compelling address. Unfortunately he disfigured it with a narrow and jealous approach to the question, of political motives, stating that his party alone had the interests of the people at heart, and imputing improper motives to all other hon. members in this house. I also wish to offer my congratulations to the Minister of Finance with regard to the announcement on Monday, October 22, wherein he stated, referring to the government's proposals as found at page 810 of Hansard:
Perhaps the most important development of all is the national economic development board.
These are noble words, Mr. Chairman, but may I say that we view them from this side of the house with some skepticism. It is within the recollection of the minister himself that on May 23, 1960 a similar proposal was made from this side of the house, and when the suggestion was put forth it was sacked and sabotaged by those who now occupy the government benches. The resolution advanced at that time by the hon. member for Essex East at page 4142 of Hansard for 1960 recommended that steps be taken-
-for the immediate setting up of a national advisory board on economic development.
This is what the present government said in reply to that motion. I am quoting, now, from Hansard at page 4163 of the same year

where the Minister of Labour is reported as saying:
On that committee he wants-
He was referring to the hon. member for Essex East.
-representatives of government, industry, labour, agriculture and the universities to serve. On that ground alone I submit that because of the diversity of interests the job of the committee would be impossible from the very outset.
Compare this to what the Minister of Finance had to say last Monday as found on page 810 of Hansard.
It is an essential aspect of national interest to encourage and expand constructive thinking and planning about national economic development by leaders in business, in agriculture, in trade unions and in other major economic groups throughout the country.
It is apparent, now, that they must have changed their script writers since the time the Minister of Labour made his announcement. However, I congratulate the hon. gentleman that after two years of urging from this side of the house they have had another great revelation, another vision. I do not wish the minister to think that we are unappreciative or churlish on this side of the house, because we believe that long range planning is worth while. I am sure he will understand when we say we are glad that they have at least repented, because there is greater joy in the kingdom of Heaven over one Tory who repents over long range planning than there is when ten Liberals reaffirm their principles and their belief in economic planning.
I know the minister will understand and forgive us if we express certain reservations about the implementation of the national economic development board. We have had the example of ARDA which was brought in with a flourish of oratory and which has since been gathering the dust of government complacency. Let it not be doubted that ARDA could be an effective instrument, along with a national marketing board, in advancing the economic interest of this country, but it lies on the statute books without action being taken.
No doubt, the economic expansion of western Europe has been due in part to long-range planning, but we should approach long-range planning with caution. There is no magic economic healing power in planning alone. There has been held before us the vision of a western Europe whose economy has undergone a great expansion as a result of long range planning. However, this is what an authority in Great Britain said about economic planning in France-an authority which, I believe, the hon. member for York South would respect. I am quoting now, from the British Hansard, from a speech delivered

by the Right Hon. Harold Wilson, a labour member of parliament and one of the leaders of the Labour party in Britain. This is what he said on November 7, 1960:
It is right, however, to warn the house against the view that the French economic miracle of the past two years has been achieved by the system of painless planning which the chancellor has in mind. It is the product of two things-two separate devaluations in 18 months, and a 6 to 8 per cent reduction in wage standards.
I am sure the hon. member for York South, along with all other hon. members of this house, would not wish to see our economic expansion take place at the expense of wage standards.
I do not wish to be misunderstood. I am not downgrading long range economic planning. I do say that alone it has no inherent healing power which will take care of all our economic ills.
We have also been given the example of West Germany as being another nation whose prosperity is due solely to economic planning. I would draw the attention of the committee to the existence of other factors which help account for the German recovery. Perhaps the most important single influence is the fact that most of the West German factories were completely retooled and re-equipped after the war, and these new machines and techniques obviously gave Germany a tremendous advantage. Further, due to the depopulation of eastern Germany, there has been an increase of almost 15 per cent in the labour force of West Germany, much of this consisting of skilled workers. This, again, has been an important factor in West Germany's economic recovery.
Business of the House
May I say we are not going to solve our economic ills by generalities, pleasant as they may be, about long range planning. I agree that we must have a list of priorities set up. We must have a plan through which we can weigh the supply of capital and labour, the extent of our exports and imports, the extent of our resources, and so on. We must set up targets for five or six years ahead. That is what has been done in France where at present they anticipate an annual increase in the gross national product of about 5.5 per cent for the next five years. But at the top of these priorities we must place government encouragement to investigation in the scientific field. This, in my opinion, is the most vital question which faces the government today-the amount of encouragement it intends to give to scientific investigation to assist industry in this country.
Progress reported.

speechtext: May I inquire from the leader of the house what we shall be doing tomorrow? Perhaps he will project his mind to cover the rest of the week.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Tomorrow, we shall continue in committee of ways and means. Again, we hope we shall get on to the resolutions and complete them. All being well, on Thursday we shall go on to legislative items beginning with a bill to amend the Farm Credit Act and then the bill to amend the Food and Drugs Act. I will give a more precise outline tomorrow at six o'clock.
At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
